p.seg: Duke Xiào was planning state affairs,
with three senior officials—Gōngsūn Yāng, Gān Lóng, and Dù Zhì—attending the ruler,
considering the changes in world affairs,
discussing the fundamentals of proper governance,
and seeking the way to guide the people.
The ruler said:
"Succeeding to the throne without forgetting the state
is the way of a ruler;
implementing laws to clarify the sovereign's authority
is the conduct of a minister.
Now I wish to reform the laws to govern,
and change the rites to educate the people,
but I fear the world will criticize me."
Gōngsūn Yāng said:
"I have heard,
'Hesitant action achieves nothing,
hesitant endeavors bring no merit.'
Your Majesty should swiftly decide on the plan for legal reform,
with no regard for the world's criticism.
Moreover, those with superior conduct
are inevitably opposed by the world;
those with unique insights
are sure to be slandered by the people.
As the saying goes:
'The foolish are blind to accomplished facts,
the wise perceive what is yet unborn.
One cannot consult the people at the start,
but can share joy with them in success.'
Guō Yǎn's laws state:
'Those who discuss supreme virtue
do not conform to customs;
those who achieve great merit
do not consult the masses.'
Laws
are meant to love the people;
rites
are meant to facilitate affairs.
Thus, if sages can strengthen the state,
they do not follow old ways;
if they can benefit the people,
they do not adhere to old rites."
Duke Xiào said:
"Good."
Gān Lóng said:
"Not so.
I have heard that
sages do not change the people to educate them,
and the wise do not alter laws to govern.
Educating according to the people
brings success without toil;
governing based on existing laws
makes officials familiar and people content.
Now if we change the laws,
not following Qín's traditions,
and alter rites to educate the people,
I fear the world will criticize you,
and I urge careful consideration."
Gōngsūn Yāng said:
"What you speak
are conventional words.
Ordinary people cling to old habits,
scholars are mired in their learning.
These two types can hold office and maintain laws,
but cannot discuss what lies beyond laws.
The Three Dynasties ruled with different rites,
the Five Hegemons dominated with different laws.
Thus, the wise create laws,
while the foolish are constrained by them;
the worthy change rites,
while the unworthy are bound by them.
Those bound by rites
are not worth discussing affairs with;
those constrained by laws
are not worth debating change with.
Your Majesty should have no doubts."
Dù Zhì said:
"I have heard
that without hundredfold benefit,
one does not change laws;
without tenfold gain,
one does not replace tools.
I hear that emulating antiquity avoids error,
following rites prevents deviation.
I urge Your Majesty to consider this."
Gōngsūn Yāng said:
"Earlier ages had different teachings—
which antiquity should we follow?
Emperors and kings did not repeat each other—
which rites should we adhere to?
Fúxī and Shénnóng taught without punishment,
Huángdì, Yáo, and Shùn punished without wrath,
and by the time of Wén and Wǔ,
each established laws according to their era,
creating rites based on circumstances.
Rites and laws are set according to the times,
regulations suit what is appropriate,
weapons and tools serve their functions.
Thus I say:
'Governing the world requires no single way,
benefiting the state need not imitate antiquity.'
Tāng and Wǔ became kings
not by following antiquity but by rising;
Yīn and Xià perished
not for failing to change rites but by falling.
Hence, those who oppose antiquity are not necessarily wrong,
and those who follow rites are not necessarily praiseworthy.
Your Majesty should have no doubts."
Duke Xiào said:
"Good.
I hear that remote alleys breed strangeness,
biased learning fosters arguments.
The laughter of fools
is mourned by the wise;
the joy of madmen
is worried by the worthy.
Though bound by worldly opinions,
I, the ruler, have no more doubts."
Thereupon, the Order to Reclaim Wasteland was issued.
Without delayed governance,
corrupt officials cannot pursue private profit among the people,
and the affairs of all officials do not stagnate.
With unimpeded official affairs,
farmers have surplus time.
Without corrupt officials seeking private profit,
farmers are not oppressed.
Unoppressed farmers with surplus time
will surely reclaim wasteland.
Taxing based on grain estimates
unifies the ruler and equalizes the people.
Unified rule brings trust,
trust prevents officials from corruption.
Equal people are cautious,
caution makes them hard to change.
With trust and uncorrupt officials,
and cautious, stable people,
the lower classes do not oppose the ruler,
nor suffer from officials.
Without opposition to the ruler
or suffering from officials,
strong people diligently farm without change.
Strong people farming steadfastly
inspires the youth to learn endlessly.
With youth learning incessantly,
wasteland will surely be reclaimed.
Without granting ranks and offices based on external influence,
people do not overvalue scholarship,
nor undervalue farming.
Not overvaluing learning keeps people simple,
simplicity prevents external contacts,
lack of external contacts encourages diligent farming without slacking.
Not undervaluing farming
ensures state security and stability.
With state security and stability,
and diligent farming without slacking,
wasteland will surely be reclaimed.
High salaries and heavy taxes,
with many dependents,
harm farming;
thus, based on the number of dependents,
levy taxes and impose heavy labor,
so that idle and wandering people have no means to eat.
Without means to eat, they must farm,
and farming ensures wasteland reclamation.
Prevent merchants from buying grain,
and farmers from selling it.
Farmers unable to sell grain
will motivate the lazy to work hard.
Merchants unable to buy grain
gain no extra joy in plentiful years;
without extra joy in plenty,
they have no surplus profit in lean years;
no surplus profit makes merchants cautious,
caution turns them to farming.
Lazy farmers motivated,
merchants turning to farm,
ensure wasteland reclamation.
Ban music and lavish costumes in all counties,
so people work without distraction,
and rest without listening to them.
Resting without such distractions
prevents dissipated energy;
working without distraction
focuses the mind.
With focused mind and undissipated energy,
wasteland will surely be reclaimed.
Forbid hiring laborers,
so officials and patriarchs do not undertake construction.
Beloved sons do not eat idly,
the lazy are not indolent,
and hired laborers have no means to eat,
forcing them to farm.
Without construction by officials and patriarchs,
farming is unharmed.
Beloved sons not eating idly,
the lazy not indolent,
prevent existing fields from lying waste.
Farming unharmed,
farmers more devoted to farming,
ensure wasteland reclamation.
Abolish inns,
then deceitful, restless, privately connected, and agriculturally hesitant people will not travel.
Those who depend on inns will have no means of sustenance,
and will certainly turn to farming,
then the land will surely be cultivated.
Monopolize mountains and marshes,
then lazy, indolent, and greedy people will have no means of sustenance;
having no means of sustenance, they will certainly farm,
then the land will surely be cultivated.
Increase the price of wine and meat,
raise their taxes,
making them ten times the cost.
Thus, merchants will decrease,
the people cannot indulge in excessive drinking,
and high officials will not indulge in gluttony.
With fewer merchants,
the state will not waste grain;
the people cannot indulge in excessive drinking,
then farmers will not be negligent;
high officials not indulging in gluttony,
state affairs will not be delayed,
and the ruler will not make mistaken decisions.
The state not wasting grain,
the people not neglecting farming,
then the land will surely be cultivated.
Impose heavy penalties and extend their consequences,
then narrow-minded and impatient people will not fight,
stubborn and rigid people will not litigate,
lazy and idle people will not wander,
wasteful people
will not act,
and cunning, flattering, malicious people will not change.
If these five types of people do not arise within the borders,
then the land will surely be cultivated.
Prevent the people from moving freely,
then foolish and agriculturally disruptive people will have no means of sustenance and must farm.
If foolish and restless people are unified in purpose,
then farmers will certainly be settled.
Farmers settled,
foolish and disruptive people wanting to farm,
then the land will surely be cultivated.
Equalize the conscription of surplus sons for service,
assign them by hereditary duty,
and raise the requirements for exemption,
ensuring they have provisions,
officials supply rations,
making it impossible to evade service.
And since high positions cannot be guaranteed,
surplus sons will not wander serving others.
Surplus sons not wandering to serve others,
they will certainly farm,
then the land will surely be cultivated.
For the state's high officials and various officers,
broad knowledge, debate, cleverness, and leisurely activities
are all prohibited;
they cannot reside or travel in the various counties,
then farmers will have no exposure to changing ideas or methods.
Farmers having no exposure to changing ideas or methods,
then knowledgeable farmers cannot leave their traditional work,
and ignorant farmers remain unaware,
not fond of learning.
Ignorant farmers unaware,
not fond of learning,
then they will diligently farm.
Knowledgeable farmers not leaving their traditional work,
then the land will surely be cultivated.
Order army markets to have no women,
and command their merchants;
require people to supply their own armor and weapons,
making them observe military readiness.
Also ensure army markets have no private grain transporters,
then deceitful schemes will have no place to hide.
Those who stealthily transport grain will not privately hoard.
Lazy and idle people will not wander in army markets,
grain thieves will have no market.
Grain deliverers not acting privately,
lazy and idle people not wandering in army markets,
then farmers will not be corrupted,
state grain will not be depleted,
then the land will surely be cultivated.
If the administration of all counties is uniform,
then those transferring will not embellish,
successors will not dare change the system,
and those who err and are dismissed cannot conceal their actions.
Wrong actions not concealed,
then officials will have no corrupt individuals.
Transferring officials not embellishing,
successors not changing,
then bureaucracy will be reduced and the people not overburdened.
Officials without corruption then people will not roam,
people not roaming,
then livelihoods will not be ruined.
Bureaucracy reduced then levies will not be excessive,
people not overburdened then farmers have more days.
Farmers having more days,
levies not excessive,
livelihoods not ruined,
then the land will surely be cultivated.
Increase taxes on passes and markets,
then farmers will dislike merchants,
and merchants will have hesitant and lazy minds.
Farmers disliking merchants,
merchants hesitant and lazy,
then the land will surely be cultivated.
Based on merchant household numbers, conscript merchants,
ensuring their servants and laborers are properly registered,
then farmers will be at ease and merchants burdened.
Farmers at ease then good fields will not lie fallow,
merchants burdened then the礼节 of sending and receiving gifts will not permeate the counties,
then farmers will not go hungry,
and conduct will not be embellished.
Farmers not hungry,
conduct not embellished,
then public works will be diligent,
and private work will not be neglected,
then farming will certainly succeed.
Farming certainly succeeding,
then the land will surely be cultivated.
Order grain delivery without hiring transport,
without return employment;
carts, oxen, and loads prepared,
must be properly registered.
Thus, going swiftly and returning quickly,
then the task will not harm farming.
The task not harming farming,
then the land will surely be cultivated.
Do not allow pleading with officials to feed criminals,
then wicked people will have no support.
Wicked people having no support,
then wicked acts will not be encouraged.
Wicked acts not encouraged,
then wicked people will have no simplicity.
Wicked people without simplicity,
then farmers will not be ruined.
Farmers not ruined,
then the land will surely be cultivated.
Generally, what the ruler uses to encourage the people
is official ranks;
what makes the state prosper
is agriculture and warfare.
Now if people seek official ranks
not through agriculture and warfare,
but with clever words and empty talk,
this is called exhausting the people.
Those who exhaust the people,
their state will certainly lack strength.
Lacking strength,
the state will certainly be weakened.
Those skilled in governing the state,
in educating the people,
all enable them to obtain official ranks through one void.
Therefore, without agriculture and warfare,
there are no official ranks.
The state eliminates empty talk then the people are simple,
the people simple then they are not corrupted.
When the people see that benefits from above come from one void,
they will focus on one,
focusing on one then the people will not be negligent.
People not negligent or corrupted then they are strong,
strong then the state is powerful.
Now the people within the borders
all say:
"Agriculture and warfare can be avoided,
and official ranks can be obtained."
Thus, the outstanding can change occupations,
devote themselves to studying the Shī and Shū,
follow external powers,
above can gain prominence,
below can obtain official ranks;
the commoners engage in trade,
practice crafts:
all to avoid agriculture and warfare.
If this is fully realized,
the state is in danger.
If the people are taught this way,
the state will certainly be weakened.
Those skilled in governing the state,
even with full granaries,
do not neglect agriculture;
with a large state and numerous people,
not corrupted by empty talk,
then the people are simple and unified.
People simple and unified,
then official ranks cannot be obtained by clever means.
Cannot be obtained by clever means,
then wickedness does not arise.
Wickedness not arising then the ruler is not misled.
Now the people within the borders and those holding official ranks,
seeing that at court they can obtain official ranks with clever words and debates,
thus official ranks cannot be obtained consistently.
Therefore, in advancing they flatter the ruler,
in retreat they consider how to benefit themselves,
then below they sell authority.
Flattering the ruler and considering private gain,
is not beneficial to the state,
yet they do it
for the sake of rank and salary.
To sell off authority from below,
is not the act of a loyal minister,
and those who do so,
do it for the sake of material goods.
Thus, those among lower officials who hope for promotion,
all say:
"With ample goods, high officials can be won over as desired."
They say:
"If I do not serve superiors with goods to seek promotion,
it is like using a cat to bait a mouse—
certainly hopeless.
If I serve superiors with sincerity to seek promotion,
it is like pulling a broken rope to straighten warped wood—
even more hopeless.
Since neither approach leads to promotion,
how can I avoid stirring the masses below to obtain goods to serve superiors,
in order to seek promotion?"
The common people say:
"I toil diligently at farming,
first filling the public granaries,
gathering the surplus to serve my parents,
and fight forgetting life for the ruler,
to honor the sovereign and secure the state;
yet the granaries are empty,
the sovereign humbled,
my family poor—
then it is better to seek office!"
When relatives and friends gather,
they change their plans.
The ambitious study the Shī and Shū,
aligning with external powers;
the mediocre engage in trade,
practice crafts:
all to avoid farming and warfare.
If the people take this as teaching,
how can grain not diminish,
and how can the military not weaken?
Those skilled in governing a state,
have clear official laws,
thus not relying on clever schemes;
the ruler focuses on one policy,
so the people do not become idle or dissolute,
and the state's strength is consolidated.
A state with consolidated strength is strong;
a state fond of empty talk declines.
Therefore it is said:
Among a thousand people engaged in farming and warfare,
if there is one versed in the Shī, Shū, and clever debates,
all thousand will neglect farming and warfare.
Among a hundred people engaged in farming and warfare,
if there is one practicing crafts,
all hundred will neglect farming and warfare.
Then official ranks cannot be obtained by cunning means.
If they cannot be obtained cunningly,
then corruption does not arise.
The state relies on farming and warfare for security;
the ruler relies on them for honor.
If the people do not farm or fight,
it is because the ruler favors talk and officials lose their constant duties.
Constant duties lead to orderly governance;
unified focus leads to state wealth;
a wealthy and well-governed state
is the way to kingship.
Therefore it is said:
The kingly way arises
from dedicating oneself to unity.
Now if the ruler selects and appoints based on talent and wisdom,
the wise will cater to the ruler's likes and dislikes in administering affairs,
to suit the ruler's heart.
Thus, officials lack constancy,
the state falls into chaos without unity,
and debaters act without law.
In this case,
how can the people's pursuits not multiply,
and how can the land not lie waste?
Shī, Shū, rites, music, goodness, cultivation, benevolence, integrity, debate, wisdom—
if a state has these ten,
the ruler has none to defend or fight.
If the state is governed by these ten,
if enemies come, it will surely be weakened;
If the state discards these ten,
enemies dare not come;
even if they come,
they will surely retreat;
if raising troops to attack,
it will surely conquer;
if holding troops without attack,
it will surely prosper.
A state that values strength
is said to "attack with difficulty"
—attacking with difficulty ensures rise;
one fond of debate
is said to "attack with ease"—
attacking with ease ensures peril.
Thus, sages and enlightened rulers,
cannot exhaust all things,
but know the essence of all things.
Therefore, in governing the state,
they only examine the essence.
Now, those governing states often lack this essence.
In court discussions on governance,
they busily contradict each other.
Thus, the ruler is confused by theories,
officials are disordered by words,
and the people become lazy and do not farm.
Therefore, the people within its borders
all transform to love debate and learning,
engage in trade,
practice crafts,
avoiding farming and warfare.
In this case, the state's downfall is not far off.
When the state faces crisis,
the learned dislike laws,
merchants are adept at evasion,
craftsmen are not employed,
so the state is easily defeated.
With few farmers
and many idle eaters,
the state becomes poor and endangered.
Now, pests like caterpillars are born in spring and die in autumn,
yet one outbreak leaves people short of food for years.
Now, with one person farming
and a hundred eating,
this is a greater pest than caterpillars.
Even with Shī and Shū,
one bundle per village,
one copy per household,
it alone benefits not governance,
nor is it the way to reverse decline.
Thus, former kings reversed it through farming and warfare.
Therefore it is said:
With a hundred farming and
one idle,
there is kingship;
with ten farming and
one idle,
there is strength;
with half farming and half idle,
there is peril.
Thus, those governing desire the people to farm.
If the state does not farm,
it cannot sustain itself in contending for power with feudal lords,
for it lacks sufficient collective strength.
Thus, feudal lords exploit its weakness,
prey on its decline,
its land is encroached and lost without recovery,
and then it is too late.
The people's loyalty to the ruler and death for the system
come from their daily engagement in farming.
The people become unusable
when they see that rhetoricians and wandering scholars can gain honor by serving the ruler,
merchants can enrich their families,
and crafts can suffice to make a living.
When the people see these three as convenient and profitable,
they will surely avoid farming;
avoiding farming, they轻视 their settlements;
轻视 their settlements, they will not defend or fight for the ruler.
In this case, the state's downfall is not far off.
All who govern states
fear the people's dispersion and inability to consolidate,
thus sages promote unity
to consolidate them.
A state unified for one year
is strong for ten;
unified for ten years
is strong for a hundred;
unified for a hundred years
is strong for a thousand;
strong for a thousand years achieves kingship.
The ruler cultivates rewards and punishments to support unified teaching,
so the teaching has constancy,
and governance achieves success.
A king grasps the ultimate essence of governing the people,
so without waiting for rewards, the people are loyal to the ruler;
without waiting for ranks and emoluments, the people work;
without waiting for punishments, the people risk their lives.
When the state is endangered and the ruler troubled,
rhetoricians swarm in crowds,
but they benefit not safety or danger.
The state's danger and ruler's trouble
come from strong enemies and great states.
If the ruler cannot subdue strong enemies
or defeat great states,
he should strengthen defenses,
utilize terrain advantages,
consolidate the people's strength to handle external threats,
then calamity can be avoided,
and kingship attained.
Thus, enlightened rulers improve governance and promote unity,
eliminating the useless,
stopping those who pursue idle learning and dissolute activities,
uniting them in farming,
then the state can be enriched,
and the people's strength consolidated.
The rulers of today all worry about their state's peril and military weakness,
yet they forcefully listen to persuaders.
Persuaders form groups,
with verbose and ornate speeches,
yet without practical use.
The ruler enjoys their rhetoric,
not seeking their substance.
Persuaders become smug,
twisting arguments on the roads,
gathering in swarms generation after generation.
When people see that they can win over kings and nobles,
they all emulate them.
When men form cliques and debate in the state,
the common folk delight in this chaos,
and the great men enjoy it.
Thus, among such people, farmers are few,
and idle eaters are many;
when many, farmers become negligent,
and when farmers are negligent, the land lies waste.
When scholarship becomes a custom,
the people abandon farming,
engaging in talk and persuasion,
with lofty words and false debates,
leaving farming to eat idly,
and competing with speech.
Hence, the people rebel against superiors and become disloyal,
forming crowds.
This teaches poverty for the state and weakness for the military.
If a state employs people based on speech,
then the people will not engage in farming.
Thus, only an enlightened ruler knows that favoring speech cannot strengthen the military or expand territory.
Only the sage in governing the state,
focuses on one thing,
unifying it in agriculture alone.
Using strength to eliminate weakness,
leads to weakness;
using weakness to eliminate strength,
leads to strength.
If the state acts benevolently,
villains will multiply.
When a rich state acts poor,
governance is called double wealth,
and double wealth brings strength.
When a poor state acts rich,
governance is called double poverty,
and double poverty brings weakness.
If the military does what the enemy dares not do,
it is strong;
if it undertakes what the enemy is ashamed to do,
it gains profit.
The ruler values frequent changes,
the state values few changes.
If the state has few goods,
it declines;
if the state has many goods,
it is strong.
A state of a thousand chariots,
if it conserves a thousand goods, declines.
Engaging in war and using troops is called strength.
If war is chaotic and troops idle, the state declines.
Punishment generates force,
force generates strength,
strength generates authority,
authority generates benevolence,
benevolence arises from force.
Mobilizing force achieves courageous warfare,
warfare achieves wisdom and strategy.
Farming, commerce, and officials—
these three are the state's constant offices.
From these three offices arise six parasitic officials:
called year,
called food,
called beauty,
called preference,
called ambition,
called conduct,
if these six have substance, the state must decline.
The substance of the three offices lies in three people,
the substance of the six offices in one person.
Using law to eliminate law,
brings strength;
using law to invite law,
brings decline.
If constant offices and laws are removed, there is order.
Governing a large state,
make it small;
governing a small state,
make it large.
Strengthening it,
leads to heavy decline;
weakening it,
leads to heavy strength.
Farming, commerce, and officials—
these three are the state's constant offices.
From these three offices arise six parasitic officials:
called year,
called food,
called beauty,
called preference,
called ambition,
called conduct,
if these six have substance, the state must decline.
The substance of the three offices lies in three people,
the substance of the six offices in one person.
Promoting labor and appointing merit is called strength,
if parasitic officials arise, the state must decline.
If farmers are few and merchants many,
nobles become poor, merchants poor, farmers poor,
if the three offices are poor,
the state must decline.
If a state has rites and music,
has odes and documents,
has kindness and cultivation,
has filial piety and fraternal duty,
has integrity and debate—if a state has these ten,
the ruler cannot send them to war,
and it must decline to ruin;
if a state lacks these ten,
the ruler can send them to war,
and it must rise to kingship.
If a state uses good people to govern villains,
it will be chaotic to the point of decline;
if a state uses villains to govern good people,
it will be orderly to the point of strength.
If a state is governed with odes, documents, rites, music, filial piety, fraternal duty, kindness, and cultivation,
enemies will come and the state must decline,
or if they do not come, the state will be poor.
If not using these eight in governance,
enemies dare not come,
and if they do come,
they must retreat;
if raising troops to attack,
victory is certain,
and what is taken can be held;
if halting troops and not attacking,
wealth is certain.
If a state favors force,
it is said "to attack with difficulty";
if a state favors speech,
it is said "to attack with ease".
A state that attacks with difficulty,
gains ten from one effort;
one that attacks with ease,
loses a hundred from ten efforts.
Heavy penalties and light rewards,
then the ruler loves the people,
and the people die for the ruler;
heavy rewards and light penalties,
then the ruler does not love the people,
and the people do not die for the ruler.
In a rising state,
applying penalties,
the people benefit and fear;
applying rewards,
the people benefit and love.
In applying punishments, make light offenses heavy,
then light offenses do not arise,
and heavy offenses do not come.
If a state lacks force but employs wisdom and cunning,
it must perish.
Timid people, if driven by penalties, become brave;
brave people, if driven by rewards, will die.
If the timid are brave,
and the brave die,
a state with no enemies is strong,
and strong must achieve kingship.
The poor, if driven by penalties, become rich;
the rich, if driven by rewards, become poor.
If governing can make the poor rich,
and the rich poor,
then the state has abundant force,
and abundant force achieves kingship.
A kingly state uses nine parts penalty, one part reward;
a strong state, seven parts penalty, three parts reward;
a declining state, five parts penalty, five parts reward.
If a state focuses on one thing for one year,
it is strong for ten years;
if focused for ten years,
strong for a hundred years;
if focused for a hundred years,
strong for a thousand years,
and a thousand-year strong one becomes king.
Authority takes ten with one,
takes substance with reputation,
thus one who can wield authority becomes king.
Able to produce but not to kill,
is called a "self-attacking state",
and must decline;
able to produce and to kill,
is called an "enemy-attacking state",
and must be strong.
Thus, attacking offices,
attacking force,
attacking enemies—
if a state uses two of these,
abandoning one,
it must be strong;
if it employs all three,
its authority surely brings kingship.
If decisions are made at intervals of ten lǐ,
the state is weak;
if decisions are made at intervals of five lǐ,
the state is strong.
One who governs by day becomes king;
one who governs by night is strong;
one who governs overnight declines.
Record the population count,
register the living,
remove the deceased.
If the people do not evade grain taxes,
and there are no barren fields in the countryside,
then the state is wealthy;
a wealthy state is strong.
Using punishment to eliminate punishment,
the state is well-governed;
using punishment to invite punishment,
the state falls into chaos.
Hence it is said:
Impose heavy penalties for minor offenses,
punishment will be eliminated and affairs accomplished,
the state is strong;
if heavy penalties are for heavy crimes and light for minor ones,
punishments will multiply and troubles arise,
the state declines.
When money is produced, grain perishes;
when grain is produced, money perishes.
If the fundamental goods are cheap,
producers are many,
buyers are few,
farmers suffer while the cunning are encouraged;
the military weakens,
the state will inevitably decline to ruin.
For one tael of gold produced within the borders,
twelve dàn of grain are lost abroad.
For twelve dàn of grain produced within the borders,
one tael of gold is lost abroad.
If a state favors producing gold within its borders,
then both gold and grain perish,
granaries and treasuries are both empty,
the state is weak.
If a state favors producing grain within its borders,
then both gold and grain thrive,
granaries and treasuries are both full,
the state is strong.
A strong state knows thirteen statistics:
the number of granaries and households within its borders,
the number of able-bodied men and women,
the number of the elderly and weak,
the number of officials and scholars,
the number of those who make a living by persuasion,
the number of beneficial people,
the number of horses, oxen, and fodder.
To strengthen the state,
without knowing these thirteen statistics,
even with favorable terrain,
and a numerous population,
the state will grow weaker and decline.
A state with no resentful people is called strong.
Raising troops to attack,
with military ranks and appointments based on merit,
ensures victory;
halting troops to farm,
with ranks and appointments based on grain contributions,
then the state becomes wealthy.
If launching troops leads to victory over enemies,
and halting troops enriches the state,
one becomes king.
Sophistry and cleverness
are aids to chaos;
rites and music,
signs of decadence;
kindness and benevolence,
the mother of faults;
favoritism and reputation,
rats of villainy.
Chaos with aids will spread,
decadence with signs will be practiced,
faults with a mother will arise,
villainy with rats will not cease.
If these eight form groups,
the people overcome the government;
if the state lacks these eight,
the government overcomes the people.
If the people overcome the government,
the state is weak;
if the government overcomes the people,
the military is strong.
Thus, if a state has these eight,
the ruler has no means to enforce defense and warfare,
and it will inevitably decline to ruin;
if the state lacks these eight,
the ruler has means to enforce defense and warfare,
and it will inevitably rise to kingship.
Employing the good,
then the people cherish their kin;
employing the cunning,
then the people adhere to the system.
To unite and restore them
is goodness;
* *to separate and monitor them
is cunning.
Promoting goodness leads to hidden faults,
employing the cunning ensures crimes are punished.
Hidden faults mean the people overcome the law,
punished crimes mean the law overcomes the people.
If the people overcome the law,
the state is chaotic;
if the law overcomes the people,
the military is strong.
Hence it is said:
Governing with good people,
will lead to chaos and decline;
governing with cunning people,
will lead to order and strength.
Punishment generates strength,
strength generates power,
power generates authority,
authority generates might,
might originates from punishment.
Thus, more punishments mean heavier rewards,
fewer rewards mean heavier punishments.
The people have desires and aversions,
desires include six excesses,
aversions include four hardships.
Indulging the six excesses,
the state weakens;
implementing the four hardships,
the military strengthens.
If the state attacks with hardships,
one move gains ten;
if the state attacks with ease,
ten moves lose a hundred.
A state that values strength
is said:
"to attack with hardships";
a state that values empty talk
is said:
"to attack with ease".
The people are easily persuaded,
but hard to employ.
Thus, the king applies punishment in nine cases,
and reward in one.
Punishment in nine cases
stops the six excesses;
reward in one case
implements the four hardships.
If the six excesses stop,
the state has no villainy;
if the four hardships are implemented,
the military is invincible.
If state laws make people endure hardships,
and the military uses what people find easy,
attacking with strength
yields one move gaining ten.
If state laws make people follow ease,
and the military uses what people find hard,
attacking with words
results in ten moves losing a hundred.
Heavy penalties
make ranks esteemed;
light rewards
make punishments威严.
Esteemed ranks
make the ruler care for the people;
威严 punishments
make the people die for the ruler.
Thus, a rising state implementing penalties benefits the people,
using rewards makes the ruler respected.
Detailed laws lead to numerous punishments,
simple laws lead to few punishments.
If the people are not governed, chaos arises;
governing them in chaos leads to further chaos.
Thus, governing them in order
brings order;
governing them in chaos
brings chaos.
The nature of the people is orderly,
but their affairs become chaotic.
Therefore, in applying punishments,
impose heavy penalties for minor offenses;
if minor offenses do not arise,
then major ones have no way to occur.
This is called "governing in order".
Applying punishments,
heavily penalizing major offenses,
lightly penalizing minor ones;
if minor offenses do not cease,
then major ones cannot be stopped.
This is called "governing in chaos".
Thus, heavy penalties for minor offenses
eliminate punishment and accomplish affairs,
the state is strong;
heavy for heavy and light for light,
then punishments multiply and troubles arise,
the state declines.
When the people are brave,
reward them with what they desire;
when the people are timid,
punish them with what they hate.
Thus, if the timid are governed with punishments,
they become brave;
if the brave are governed with rewards,
they will die [for the state].
When the timid become brave,
and the brave are willing to die,
a state with no rivals is sure to rule the world.
When the people are poor, they are weak;
when the state is rich, they become licentious;
licentiousness breeds parasites,
and parasites lead to weakness.
Thus, if the poor are enriched through punishments,
they become wealthy;
if the wealthy are reduced through rewards,
they become poor.
The measure of governing a state
values making the poor rich,
and the rich poor.
When the poor become rich,
and the rich become poor,
the state is strong.
If the three officials have no parasites,
the state is strong;
and if it remains free of parasites for long,
it is sure to rule the world.
The people have myriad desires,
but benefits come from a single source.
Without this one source, the people cannot attain their desires,
so they devote themselves to one pursuit.
Devotion to one pursuit concentrates their strength,
and concentrated strength makes the state strong;
when strength is employed,
it becomes doubly strong.
Thus, the ability to generate strength,
and to expend strength,
is called:
"attacking enemy states,"
and such a state will surely be powerful.
Block private paths to stifle their ambitions,
open one gate to fulfill their desires,
making the people first endure what they hate,
and only then attain what they desire,
so their strength multiplies.
If strength multiplies but is not used, ambitions are stifled,
stifled ambitions lead to selfishness,
and selfishness leads to weakness.
Thus, the ability to generate strength,
but not to expend it,
is called:
"a state attacking itself,"
and it will surely decline.
Therefore, it is said that in a true king's state, strength is not hoarded,
and households do not store grain.
The state not hoarding strength
means it is used by the people;
households not storing grain
means it is collected by the ruler.
In governing the state:
if decisions are made by households, the state rules the world;
if by officials, the state is strong;
if by the ruler alone, the state is weak.
When severe punishments for minor offenses are abolished,
and constant official duties are maintained, there is order.
Reducing penalties and ensuring mutual guarantees,
rewards must not be doubled.
If all wrongdoers are necessarily reported,
then the people will decide matters in their hearts.
When the ruler issues orders and the people know how to respond,
and tools made in households are used by the government,
then affairs are decided by households.
Thus, in a true king's state, punishments and rewards are decided in the people's hearts,
and tools are decided by households.
When governance is clear, there is unity;
when governance is obscure, there is division.
Unity leads to action,
division leads to stagnation.
Action brings order,
stagnation brings chaos.
Order means decisions by households,
chaos means decisions by the ruler.
Therefore, in a true king's state, punishments and rewards are decided in the people's hearts,
and tools are decided by households.
When governance is clear, there is unity;
when governance is obscure, there is division.
Unity leads to action,
division leads to stagnation.
Action brings order,
stagnation brings chaos.
Order means decisions by households,
chaos means decisions by the ruler.
The common failing of worldly rulers is
that in using military force, they do not assess their strength,
and in cultivating wastelands, they do not measure the land.
Thus, some have limited land but many people,
where the people overwhelm the land;
others have vast land but few people,
where the land overwhelms the people.
Where the people overwhelm the land,
focus on opening up [new land];
where the land overwhelms the people,
focus on attracting settlers.
Opening up land doubles efforts.
If people exceed the land,
state achievements are few and military strength is low;
if land exceeds people,
the wealth of mountains and marshes goes unused.
To waste natural resources
and indulge the people's licentiousness
is the error of worldly rulers,
and both high and low engage in it,
so the people are numerous but the military is weak,
and the land is vast but strength is small.
Thus, in managing land for the state,
mountains and hills should occupy one-tenth,
marshes and lakes one-tenth,
valleys and flowing water one-tenth,
cities and roads one-tenth,
poor fields two-tenths,
and good fields four-tenths.
This is the proper law of the ancient kings,
so for the state, the number of fields divided is small.
Five hundred mǔ per person
is sufficient for one campaign,
but this land is not fully utilized.
In a territory of a hundred lǐ square,
fielding ten thousand soldiers
is a small number.
This is because the cultivated land is enough to feed the people,
cities and roads are enough to house them,
mountains, marshes, valleys, and streams are enough to provide benefits,
and marshes with dams are enough for storage.
Thus, when the army marches out,
supplies are provided and wealth is abundant;
when the army rests,
the people work and stores are ample.
This is called the law of utilizing land and preparing for campaigns.
Nowadays, rulers have territories thousands of lǐ square,
yet food is insufficient to supply campaigns and fill granaries,
and the military becomes subservient to neighboring enemies,
so this is a worry for rulers.
Having vast land but not cultivating it
is the same as having no land;
having many people but not using them
is the same as having no people.
Thus, the method for governing a state
lies in reclaiming wastelands;
the way of using military force
lies in uniform rewards.
If private profits are blocked externally,
the people will devote themselves to farming;
devotion to farming makes them simple,
and simplicity makes them fear orders.
If private rewards are prohibited among the people,
then the people's
strength is concentrated against the enemy,
and concentration against the enemy brings victory.
How do we know this is so?
By the nature of the people:
simplicity makes them labor and exert strength easily,
while poverty makes them shrewd and calculating.
Exerting strength easily makes them fearless of death and willing to be used,
calculating makes them fear punishment and endure hardship easily.
Enduring hardship easily exhausts the land's potential,
and willingness to be used exhausts military strength.
Those who govern the state and can exhaust the land's potential and make the people die [for it]
will gain both fame and profit.
In people's lives,
they seek food when hungry,
rest when tired,
pleasure when suffering,
and honor when humiliated—
this is the nature of the people.
In seeking profit,
they lose the rules of propriety;
in seeking fame,
they lose the constants of human nature.
How can we argue this?
Consider thieves and bandits: they violate the ruler's prohibitions above
and fail in the rituals of subjects below,
so their names are shamed and their lives endangered,
yet they do not stop—
for the sake of profit.
Some scholars of ancient times
wore clothes that did not warm their skin,
ate food that did not fill their bellies,
tormented their wills,
exhausted their limbs,
and harmed their internal organs,
yet their minds grew broader and more ample.
It is not the constancy of human nature,
but rather the actions taken,
that are driven by reputation.
Hence it is said: where fame and profit converge,
the people will follow.
The ruler who holds the handle of fame and profit,
and can achieve merit and reputation,
does so through method.
The sage examines authority to grasp the handle,
and examines method to employ the people.
Method is the technique of ministers and rulers,
and the essence of the state.
Thus, for a state of ten thousand chariots to lose method and not be endangered,
or for ministers and rulers to lose technique and not fall into chaos,
has never happened.
Nowadays, rulers wish to expand territory and govern the people but do not examine method,
and ministers wish to exhaust their duties but do not establish technique.
Thus, the state has disobedient people,
and the ruler has unruly ministers.
Therefore, when the sage governs the state,
internally he orders the people to devote themselves to farming,
externally he orders the people to plan for war.
Farming is what the people find bitter;
and war,
is what the people consider perilous.
To impose what they find bitter,
and compel them to face what they consider perilous,
requires calculation.
For the people, in life, calculate profit,
and in death, consider fame.
The sources of fame and profit
must be carefully examined.
If profit comes from the land,
then the people will exert their strength;
if fame comes from war,
then the people will face death.
Internally, making the people exert their strength
ensures that fields are not left barren;
externally, making the people face death
ensures that enemies are defeated.
With enemies defeated and fields not barren,
the achievement of wealth and power
can be attained effortlessly.
But now it is not so.
What contemporary rulers focus on
are none of the state's urgent needs.
Though they possess the conduct of Yáo and Shùn,
their achievements do not match the strategies of Tāng and Wǔ—
this is the fault of how they hold the handle.
I beg to speak of their errors.
If in governing the state, one abandons power and relies on rhetoric,
then the ruler toils with little achievement.
Thus, if one patronizes scholars of the Odes and Documents and rhetoricians,
the people become idle and disrespect their superiors;
if one employs recluses,
the people become aloof and criticize their superiors;
if one employs brave warriors,
the people become competitive and disregard prohibitions;
if artisans and craftsmen are used, the people become restless and easily move;
if merchants are at leisure and profit,
the people become dependent and criticize their superiors.
Thus, if these five types of people are added to state employment,
then fields become barren and the military weak.
Rhetoricians
rely on their mouths;
recluses,
rely on their ideas;
brave warriors,
rely on their courage;
artisans and craftsmen,
rely on their hands;
merchants,
rely on their persons.
Thus, though the world is one dwelling,
they encircle themselves with resources as people;
with resources valued more than their persons,
they partially rely on external power.
To carry heavy resources,
and return to a biased household—
even Yáo and Shùn would find it difficult;
thus Tāng and Wǔ prohibited it,
and thereby achieved merit and established fame.
The sage does not use what the world finds easy
to overcome what it finds difficult;
he must use what it finds difficult
to overcome what it finds easy.
Thus, if the people are ignorant,
knowledge can overcome them;
if the world is knowledgeable,
force can overcome it.
When the people are ignorant,
they are easily controlled by force but hard to guide with skill;
when the world is skillful,
they are easily guided by knowledge but hard to control with force.
Thus, Shénnóng taught farming and ruled the world,
becoming their teacher through knowledge;
Tāng and Wǔ achieved strength and subjugated the feudal lords,
making them submit through force.
Now the world is skillful and the people are dissolute,
yet we imitate the times of Tāng and Wǔ,
and pursue the tasks of Shénnóng,
following worldly prohibitions—
hence a state of a thousand chariots is confused and chaotic.
This is because what they focus on
is mistaken.
The nature of the people
is to measure and take the longer,
weigh and take the heavier,
and balance to seek profit.
An enlightened ruler carefully observes these three,
then the governance of the state can be established,
and the people's abilities can be harnessed.
What the state demands of the people is little,
but how the people avoid these demands is manifold.
Internally, make the people devoted to farming,
externally, make the people unified in war.
Thus, in the sage's governance,
he uses many prohibitions to curb abilities,
and employs force to exhaust disputes—
using both partially ensures the people within the borders are unified;
unified, the people farm,
farming makes them simple,
simplicity makes them settled and averse to leaving.
Therefore, when the sage governs the state,
the people's resources are stored in the land,
and they partially rely on peril externally.
Resources in the land bring simplicity,
reliance on peril externally brings confusion.
When the people are inward, they are simple;
when outward, they are confused—
thus they are diligent in farming and restrained in war.
If the people are diligent in farming, resources are heavy;
if restrained in war, neighbors are endangered.
Heavy resources cannot be carried off in flight;
endangered neighbors offer no refuge without resources.
To return to peril and rely externally—
even a madman would not do it.
The ruler who holds the handle of fame and profit,
and can achieve merit and reputation,
does so through method.
The sage examines authority to grasp the handle,
and examines method to employ the people.
Method is the technique of ministers and rulers,
and the essence of the state.
Thus, for a state of ten thousand chariots to lose method and not be endangered,
or for ministers and rulers to lose technique and not fall into chaos,
has never happened.
Punishments are used to prohibit evil;
and rewards,
are used to assist prohibition.
Shame, disgrace, toil, and suffering
are what the people detest;
glory, honor, ease, and pleasure
are what the people pursue.
Thus, if in a state, punishments are not feared and ranks and emoluments are not worth pursuing,
this is an omen of a perishing state.
If criminals are repeatedly pardoned,
then petty men avoid restraint and do not suffer punishment,
and they gamble on rising among the people.
Gambling on rising among the people to seek profit,
with multiple gates to glory and honor,
then noble men rely on power to achieve fame.
If petty men do not avoid prohibitions,
punishments become frequent;
if noble men do not establish orders,
penalties are enforced.
When punishments are frequent and penalties enforced,
the state is full of villainy;
when the state is full of villainy, the rich cannot guard their wealth,
and the poor cannot attend to their work—
fields become barren and the state poor.
Barren fields lead to disputes among the people,
state poverty leads to depleted rewards from above.
Therefore, in the sage's governance,
criminals hold no state positions,
and the condemned have no official appointments.
If criminals have rank,
then noble men feel ashamed of their positions;
if the condemned wear silk and eat meat,
then petty men covet their profits.
If noble men are ashamed of their positions,
they disdain merit;
if petty men covet profits,
they boast of villainy.
Thus, punishments and executions
are used to stop villainy;
and offices and ranks,
are used to encourage merit.
Now, if the state establishes ranks but the people are ashamed of them,
and sets up punishments but the people delight in them,
this is the flaw of methods and techniques.
Therefore, the noble man wields power
to unify governance and establish technique,
setting up offices and valuing ranks to match it,
evaluating toil and promoting merit to appoint them—
then the balance between superior and inferior is even.
When the balance between superior and inferior is even,
ministers can exhaust their strength,
and the ruler can monopolize the handle.
Heaven and Earth were established,
and the people were born.
At this time,
the people knew their mothers but not their fathers,
and their way was to cherish their kin and love selfishness.
Cherishing kin leads to distinctions,
loving selfishness leads to danger,
and when the multitude of people focus on distinctions and danger,
then the people become chaotic.
At this time,
the people strove to overcome and contended by force.
Striving to overcome leads to conflict,
contending by force leads to disputes,
and disputes without justice
prevent people from realizing their nature.
Therefore, the wise established impartial justice,
set aside selfishness,
and the people delighted in benevolence.
At this time,
cherishing kin was abandoned,
and honoring the worthy was established.
All benevolent people focus on love and benefit,
while the worthy take surpassing others as their way.
With a large population and no regulations,
and over time taking surpassing as the way,
chaos arises.
Therefore, the sage succeeded them,
creating divisions of land, goods, wealth, men, and women.
With divisions set but no regulations,
it is not feasible,
so prohibitions were established.
With prohibitions established but no one to enforce them,
it is not feasible,
so officials were appointed.
With officials appointed but no unity,
it is not feasible,
so a ruler was established.
Once the ruler was established,
then honoring the worthy was abandoned,
and esteeming the noble was established.
Thus, in ancient times, they cherished kin and loved selfishness;
in middle times, they honored the worthy and delighted in benevolence;
in later times, they esteemed the noble and respected officials.
Honoring the worthy
involves surpassing through excellence;
but establishing a ruler
renders worthiness useless.
Cherishing kin
takes selfishness as the way,
while impartial justice prevents selfishness from prevailing.
These three
are not contradictory practices;
rather, the people's way deteriorates and their focus shifts,
as worldly affairs change and the ways of conduct differ.
Therefore, it is said:
"The way of kings has its standards."
The way of kings is one end,
and the way of ministers is another;
their paths differ,
but the standards are the same.
Therefore, it is said:
"When the people are ignorant,
wisdom can rule the world;
when the world is wise,
strength can rule the world."
When the people are ignorant,
they have abundant strength but insufficient wisdom;
when the world is wise,
they have abundant cleverness but insufficient strength.
The nature of people is such that
when they lack knowledge, they learn;
when their strength is exhausted, they submit.
Thus, Shénnóng taught farming and ruled the world,
being followed for his wisdom;
Tāng and Wǔ achieved strength and subdued the feudal lords,
being submitted to for their power.
When the people are ignorant,
they do not possess knowledge and inquire;
when the world is wise,
they have no surplus strength and submit.
Therefore, those who rule the world with love
abolish punishments;
those who subdue feudal lords by force
set aside virtue.
The sage does not model on antiquity,
nor does he adhere to the present.
Modeling on antiquity falls behind the times,
adhering to the present obstructs the momentum.
Zhōu did not model on Shāng,
Xià did not model on Yú,
the three dynasties had different circumstances,
yet all could rule the world.
Thus, rising to kingship has its way,
but maintaining it follows different principles.
King Wǔ took power by rebellion but valued obedience,
contended for the world but esteemed yielding;
he seized it by force,
but maintained it with righteousness.
In the present age, strong states engage in annexation,
weak states strive to defend by force;
they do not reach the times of Yú and Xià above,
nor do they follow the ways of Tāng and Wǔ below.
The ways of Tāng and Wǔ are blocked,
so states with ten thousand chariots all wage war,
states with a thousand chariots all defend.
This way has been blocked for a long time,
and the rulers of the world cannot open it,
hence the three dynasties are not followed by a fourth.
Unless one is an enlightened ruler, none can listen,
and today I wish to explain it with evidence.
The people of old were simple and honest,
the people of today are clever and deceitful.
Therefore, for ancient times,
virtue was prioritized for governance;
for the present age,
punishment is prioritized for law;
this is what confuses the world.
What the present world calls righteousness
seeks to establish what the people like
and abolish what they dislike;
what they call unrighteousness
seeks to establish what the people dislike
and abolish what they enjoy.
These two are confused in name and reversed in reality,
and must be carefully examined.
Establishing what the people enjoy
leads them to suffer from what they dislike;
establishing what they dislike
leads them to be secure in what they enjoy.
How do we know this is so?
When people are anxious, they think,
and thinking leads to measures;
when they are joyful, they become indulgent,
and indulgence leads to idleness.
Therefore, governing with punishment makes the people cautious,
caution prevents wickedness,
and without wickedness, the people are secure in their joys.
Teaching with righteousness makes the people unrestrained,
unrestraint leads to chaos,
and chaos makes the people suffer from what they dislike.
What I call punishment
is the foundation of righteousness;
what the world calls righteousness
is the way of violence.
To correct the people:
by using what they dislike,
they will ultimately achieve what they like;
by using what they like,
they will surely ruin themselves with what they dislike.
Well-governed states have more punishments and fewer rewards,
chaotic states have more rewards and fewer punishments.
Therefore, a true king uses nine parts punishment and one part reward,
while a declining state uses nine parts reward and one part punishment.
As faults have severity and mildness,
punishments have lightness and heaviness;
as good deeds have greatness and smallness,
rewards have abundance and scarcity.
These two
are commonly used in the world.
The sage does not model on antiquity,
nor does he adhere to the present.
Modeling on antiquity falls behind the times,
adhering to the present obstructs the momentum.
Zhōu did not model on Shāng,
Xià did not model on Yú,
the three dynasties had different circumstances,
yet all could rule the world.
Thus, rising to kingship has its way,
but maintaining it follows different principles.
Governing the people so that great evils do not arise
and minor faults are not overlooked
leads to a well-ordered state,
and a well-ordered state must be strong.
If one state practices this,
it alone is well-ordered within its borders;
if two states practice it,
military conflicts somewhat cease;
if the whole world practices it,
the highest virtue is restored.
This is how I demonstrate that punishment reverts to virtue,
and righteousness aligns with violence.
In ancient times, people lived in clusters and groups, leading to chaos,
hence they sought to have rulers.
Thus, the world's desire to have rulers
is for the sake of order.
Now, having a ruler without laws
is as harmful as having no ruler;
having laws that cannot overcome chaos
is the same as having no laws.
The world does not feel secure without a ruler,
yet delights in overcoming the laws,
which the entire world finds perplexing.
Nothing benefits the people under heaven more greatly
than order;
and no order is more prosperous than establishing a ruler;
the way to establish a ruler,
finds no broader means than prevailing laws;
the task of prevailing laws,
knows no greater urgency than eliminating villainy;
the root of eliminating villainy,
lies none deeper than severe punishments.
Thus, the king uses rewards to prohibit,
and employs punishments to encourage;
seeking out faults rather than virtues,
relying on punishments to eliminate punishments.
In establishing a state,
its institutions must be timely,
its governing laws must be deliberate,
its state affairs must be meticulous,
and its fundamental tasks must be focused.
When institutions are timely,
the state's customs can be transformed,
and the people will follow the regulations.
When governing laws are clear,
then officials will be free of corruption.
When state affairs are unified,
the people will respond and be employed.
When fundamental tasks are focused,
the people will delight in farming and enjoy warfare.
The sages establish laws and transform customs,
making the people engage in farming from dawn to dusk,
which must not be overlooked.
2 The people follow -i- regulations unto death,
because the superiors set glorious reputations,
and establish clear rewards and punishments.
Without employing sophistry or private influence, achievements are made,
hence the people delight in farming and enjoy warfare.
Seeing the superiors honor the farmers and warriors,
while looking down on sophists and artisans,
and despising wandering scholars,
the people thus unify their efforts;
their families will surely prosper,
and they themselves will gain prominence in the state.
The superiors open public benefits and block private channels,

private labors are not recognized in the state,
