If thus achievements and fame encourage,
then the superiors' orders are carried out and wastelands are cultivated,
dissolute people cease and villainy does not sprout.
A state that can focus the people's strength and unify their efforts is strong,
one that can attend to fundamentals and restrict non-essentials is wealthy.
The sages in governing the state,
can concentrate strength,
and can expend strength.
When institutions are discerning, the people's strength is focused,
but if focused without transformation, it cannot be applied,
and if applied without enrichment, disorder arises.
Therefore, those who govern the state,
in focusing strength,
do so to enrich the state and strengthen the military;
without employing sophistry or private influence, achievements are made,
hence the people delight in farming and enjoy warfare.
Seeing the superiors honor the farmers and warriors,
while looking down on sophists and artisans,
and despising wandering scholars,
the people thus unify their efforts;
their families will surely prosper,
and they themselves will gain prominence in the state.
Governing a state values unifying the people;
when unified, the people become simple,
simplicity leads to farming,
farming makes them easily diligent,
diligence brings wealth.
The wealthy are restrained by ranks,
preventing extravagance;
the extravagant are suppressed by punishments and compelled to farm.
The superiors open public benefits and block private channels,
to mobilize the people's strength,
private labors are not recognized in the state,
and private requests are not made to the ruler.
If thus achievements and fame encourage,
then the superiors' orders are carried out and wastelands are cultivated,
dissolute people cease and villainy does not sprout.
A state that can focus the people's strength and unify their efforts is strong,
one that can attend to fundamentals and restrict non-essentials is wealthy.
When the people are not well-governed,
it is due to the ruler's way being debased;
when laws are not clear,
it is because the ruler fosters disorder.
Thus, an enlightened ruler does not debase the way,
nor foster disorder,
but holds authority firmly,
establishes laws and governs,
so as to detect villainy from above and ensure no official misconduct,
with decisive rewards and punishments and regulated use of resources.
If so, the state's systems are clear and the people's strength is exhausted,
the superiors' ranks are honored and all classes are mobilized.
Nowadays, rulers all wish to govern the people,
yet they assist in disorder;
not that they delight in causing disorder,
but they cling to old ways without observing the times.
Thus, above, they emulate antiquity and encounter obstructions,
below, they adhere to the present without timely adaptation,
failing to understand the changes in customs,
and not examining the realities of governing the people,
85 hence excessive rewards lead to punishments, - -
and light punishments eliminate rewards.
When the superiors set punishments but the people do not submit,
rewards become depleted and villainy increases.
Therefore, in dealing with the people,
the ruler prioritizes punishments over rewards.
Thus, the sages in governing the state,
do not model on antiquity,
nor adhere to the present,
but adapt governance to the era,
and establish laws according to customs.
If laws are established without examining the people's realities,
they will not succeed;
if governance suits the time and is implemented,
it will not encounter opposition.
Hence, the rule of sage kings,
is cautious in examining affairs,
and focuses the mind on unity alone.
Your minister has heard that in ancient times, enlightened rulers,
by implementing laws, the people had no villainy,
by undertaking tasks, talents were naturally honed,
by executing rewards, the military was strengthened,
these three are the foundations of governance.
That implementing laws leads to no villainy among the people,
is because laws are clear and benefit the people.
That undertaking tasks hones talents naturally,
is due to clear distinction of merits;
clear distinction of merits makes the people exert their strength,
and when the people exert their strength, talents are naturally honed.
That executing rewards strengthens the military,
refers to ranks and emoluments;
ranks and emoluments,
are the substance of the military.
Therefore, when a ruler bestows ranks and emoluments,
the way must be clear;
if the way is clear,
the state daily grows stronger;
if the way is obscure,
the state daily declines.
Thus, the way ranks and emoluments are bestowed,
is the pivot of survival or demise.
Those states that decline and rulers who perish,
do not lack ranks and emoluments,
but their way of bestowing them is erroneous.
The Three Kings and Five Hegemons,
their means were none other than ranks and emoluments,
yet their achievements differed vastly,
because their way was clear.
Therefore, an enlightened ruler in employing his ministers,
appointments must arise from their labors,
rewards must be added for their merits.
When merits and rewards are clear,
the people compete for achievements.
If a state can make its people exert strength to compete for achievements,
then the military will surely be strong.
Those of equal status becoming servants to others,
is a matter of wealth and poverty.
Those of equal substance annexing each other,
is a matter of strength and weakness.
Having land yet the ruler being sometimes strong, sometimes weak,
is a matter of order and disorder.
If there is a way and territory,
land sufficient to accommodate life,
scholars and people can be attracted.
If there is market access,
wealth and goods can be accumulated.
Those who have land cannot speak of poverty,
those who have people cannot speak of weakness.
If land is truly utilized,
there is no worry about lacking wealth;
if people are truly employed,
there is no fear of strong bullies.
When virtue is clear and teachings are practiced,
one can use what the people have,
for one's own purposes.
Thus, enlightened rulers use what is not theirs,
and employ people not originally theirs.
What enlightened rulers value,
is solely conferring ranks based on reality,
──conferring ranks based on reality and honoring them.
Without honor, there is no urgency;
if positions are not prominent,
the people will not strive for ranks.
If ranks are easily obtained,
the people will not value the superiors' ranks.
If ranks, emoluments, and rewards do not come through their proper gate,
then the people will not risk death to contend for positions.
Human nature has likes and dislikes;
thus the people can be governed.
The ruler cannot fail to examine likes and dislikes;
for likes and dislikes
are the foundation of rewards and punishments.
Now, by nature, people like ranks and emoluments and dislike penalties and punishments.
The ruler establishes these two to control the people's will
and set up what is desired.
When the people exhaust their strength and rank follows accordingly,
when achievements are established and rewards follow accordingly,
if the ruler can make his people trust in this as clearly as the sun and moon,
then the military will be invincible.
There are cases where the ruler confers ranks but the military is weak,
where emoluments are granted but the state is poor,
where laws are established but governance is chaotic.
These three
are the state's calamities.
Thus, if the ruler gives priority to personal connections and petitions,
and only afterward to merit and effort,
then ranks are conferred but the military is weak.
If the people do not risk death to face difficulties,
yet benefits and emoluments can be obtained,
then emoluments are granted but the state is poor.
If laws lack standards and measures,
and affairs grow increasingly troublesome,
then laws are established but governance is chaotic.
Therefore, the enlightened ruler in employing his people
ensures they must exert full effort to plan for their achievements,
and when achievements are established, wealth and honor follow,
with no private favors,
so education and transformation succeed.
In this way,
ministers are loyal and the ruler is enlightened,
governance is illustrious and the military strong.
Thus, whenever an enlightened ruler governs,
he relies on their strength, not their virtue,
and thus without worry or toil, achievements can be established.
Once standards and measures are established,
laws can be perfected.
Therefore, the ruler cannot but be cautious of himself.
Lì Zhū could see the tip of an autumn hair from a hundred paces away,
yet could not exchange his bright eyes with others;
Wū Huó could lift a weight of a thousand jūn,
yet could not exchange his great strength with others.
The sage's inherent nature and constitution
cannot be exchanged with others;
yet achievements can be attained—
this is what is meant by law.
In general, the methods of war must be rooted in political victory,
then the people will not contend;
without contention, there is no room for personal opinions,
and they take the superior's will as their own.
Thus, the governance of a true king
makes the people timid in local brawls
but courageous in fighting invaders.
When the people are accustomed to using force to overcome difficulties,
they lightly regard death;
seeing the enemy like a collapsing dike, unstoppable,
they flee.
Hence, the art of war says:
"In a great battle victory,
pursue the fleeing no more than ten lǐ;
in a small battle victory,
pursue the fleeing no more than five lǐ."
When raising troops, assess the enemy:
if their governance is inferior,
do not engage in battle;
if their provisions are inferior,
do not prolong the fight;
if the enemy is numerous, do not be the invader;
if the enemy is inferior in all aspects,
attack without hesitation.
Thus, it is said the great principle of war lies in caution.
By evaluating the enemy and observing the masses,
victory or defeat can be known in advance.
The army of a true king
is victorious without arrogance,
defeated without resentment.
Victorious without arrogance
is due to clear strategy;
defeated without resentment
is due to knowing what was lost.
If the military strength is equal,
a worthy general leads to victory,
an unworthy general leads to defeat.
If the strategy comes from temple calculations,
a worthy general wins,
and an unworthy general also wins.
A state that long maintains victorious strategies
will surely become strong and reach kingly status.
If the people are obedient and heed the superior,
then the state will be wealthy and the military victorious;
practicing this,
one will surely rule long as king.
The faults are:
having no enemy to match,
penetrating deeply, relying on perilous barriers and remote passes,
with the people weary, hungry, and thirsty,
and again encountering disease—
this is the path to defeat.
Therefore, in leading the people as if driving fine horses,
one cannot fail to regulate them properly.
In general, employing the military,
victory has three grades:
if before raising troops, laws are established,
laws established and customs formed,
customs formed and equipment prepared—
these three must be implemented within the borders,
and only then can troops be dispatched.
Implementing these three has two conditions:
first, assisting the law so that it is enforced;
second, ensuring actions are certain to succeed so that the law is upheld.
Thus, relying on numbers is called patchwork;
relying on elaborate preparations is called cleverness;
relying on reputation and appearance is called obstinacy.
Relying on any one of these three,
one's army can be captured.
Therefore, it is said the strong must fortify their will to fight:
when fighting, exert full strength;
with full strength exerted, preparedness is achieved.
Thus, they are invincible within the seas.
Good governance leads to accumulation of goods,
accumulation of goods enables heavy rewards.
Hence, the strong must be well-governed,
the well-governed must be strong;
the wealthy must be well-governed,
the well-governed must be wealthy;
the strong must be wealthy,
the wealthy must be strong.
Therefore, it is said the way to good governance and strength has three aspects,
discussing its fundamentals.
Unified rewards make ranks respected,
ranks respected make rewards beneficial.
Thus it is said:
The military arises from governance and differs,
customs arise from laws and transform endlessly,
surpassing power is rooted in the mind and adorned with prepared force.
If these three are properly discussed,
strength can be established.
A state facing war on four fronts
values defensive warfare;
a state backed by the sea
values offensive warfare.
A state facing war on four fronts
that likes to raise armies
to resist its four neighbors
will be in peril.
If the four neighboring states each initiate an action,
and one raises armies four times in response,
it is said the state is in peril.
A state facing war on four fronts
that cannot garrison a massive army in a city of ten thousand households
will be in peril.
Therefore, it is said:
A state facing war on four fronts
must focus on defensive warfare.
Defending a walled city
is best done with the strength of those prepared to die,
fighting against the invader's fresh strength.
If the city is hard to capture,
it is due to the strength of those prepared to die;
if the invaders do not completely level the city,
they have no way to enter;
this is called using the strength of the dead to fight the invader's living strength.
If the city is completely leveled,
and the invaders find a way in,
then the invaders will be exhausted,
while the defenders will be rested.
Using rested strength to fight exhausted strength
is called using the living strength of the defenders to fight the dead strength of the invaders.
It is said the danger of a besieged city
is that not all are willing to die for the city.
These three are not due to insufficient danger,
but the general's fault.
The way to defend a city
is to amass strength.
Therefore, for the invaders,
manage records and manifests,
and for the multitude of the three armies,
divide them according to the number of the invader's scout chariots.
The three armies are:
robust men as one army,
robust women as one army,
and the elderly and weak of both sexes as one army—
these are called the three armies.
The army of able-bodied men,
should be well-fed and sharpen their weapons,
arrayed and awaiting the enemy.
The army of able-bodied women,
should be well-fed and carry fortifications,
arrayed and awaiting orders.
When the enemy arrives, they should create earthworks to form obstacles and set traps like pitfalls,
dismantle bridges and tear down houses,
providing for relocation if possible,
then relocate;
if relocation is not feasible, burn them,
so the enemy cannot use them to aid their attack preparations.
The army of the old and weak,
should herd oxen, horses, sheep, and swine;
gather edible grasses and water sources,
collect and consume them,
to secure food for the able-bodied men and women.
Carefully ensure that the three armies do not intermix.
If able-bodied men enter the women's army,
men will value women,
and treacherous people may follow conspiracies, leading to the state's ruin;
joy and fear arise,
early rumors spread,
and brave people refuse to fight.
If able-bodied men and women enter the army of the old and weak,
the old will cause the able-bodied to grieve,
the weak will make the strong pity them,
with grief and pity in their hearts,
brave people will reconsider,
and timid people will not fight.
Therefore, it is said: carefully ensure the three armies do not intermix,
this is the way to accumulate strength.
Strict orders ensure governance without delay,
fair laws mean officials have no corruption.
Once laws are established,
do not harm them with fine words.
Appointing based on merit reduces people's talk,
appointing based on goodness increases people's talk.
Implementing laws requires decisiveness:
those who decide within five li will rule as kings,
within ten li will be strong,
delayed governance leads to decline.
Govern with punishment,
reward for battle.
Seek faults, not virtues.
Thus, laws established and not changed,
will expose people's cunning schemes,
cunning schemes cease,
distinctions are made clearly,
officials' noble ranks,
and generous salaries are based on their achievements.
If the state has no treacherous people,
then the capital has no corrupt markets.
If goods are abundant but non-essentials prevail,
agriculture relaxes and corruption wins,
the state will surely decline.
If people have surplus grain,
let them exchange grain for official ranks.
Official ranks must be earned by effort,
then farmers will not be idle.
A four-inch pipe without a bottom,
will never be full.
Granting offices and ranks, giving salaries without merit,
is like having no bottom.
A poor state that focuses on war,
directs poison to the enemy,
free from the six parasites,
will surely be strong.
A rich state that does not fight,
idles within,
harboring the six parasites,
will surely be weak.
If the state grants offices and ranks based on merit,
this is called using abundant wisdom,
and abundant courage in battle.
With abundant courage in battle,
and abundant wisdom in strategy,
the state will be invincible.
If the state grants offices and ranks based on merit,
governance is simplified and talk is reduced;
this is called using law to eliminate law,
using words to eliminate words.
If the state grants offices and ranks based on the six parasites,
governance becomes chaotic and talk arises;
this is called using law to invite law,
using words to invite words,
then the ruler busies himself with persuasive talk,
and officials are confused in managing corruption.
Corrupt ministers gain success,
the meritorious are daily pushed back,
this is called loss of control.
Adhering to ten principles brings chaos,
adhering to one brings order.
Laws are already established,
yet those who favor the six parasites will perish.
If all people farm,
the state will be rich;
if the six parasites are not used,
then soldiers and people all compete to be encouraged and gladly serve the ruler,
the people within its borders,
strive to consider it an honor,
none consider it a disgrace.
Next best is encouraged by rewards and deterred by punishments;
the worst,
people detest it,
worry about it,
are ashamed of it.
Cultivating appearances with words,
ashamed of poverty and seeking foreign ties,
to avoid farming and fighting,
relying on foreign connections for preparation,
endangers the state.
Having hunger, cold, and death,
yet not fighting for the sake of profit and salary,
this is the custom of a perishing state.
The six parasites:
are rituals and music,
poetry and books,
cultivating goodness,
filial piety and fraternal duty,
sincerity and trustworthiness,
chastity and integrity,
benevolence and righteousness,
opposing military,
and being ashamed of war.
If a state has these twelve,
the ruler cannot promote farming and fighting,
leading to poverty and decline.
If these twelve form groups,
this means the ruler's governance cannot overcome his ministers,
officials' governance cannot overcome the people,
this is called the six parasites overcoming governance.
If these twelve take root,
decline is certain.
Therefore, a rising state does not use these twelve,
so the state is powerful,
and none under heaven can invade it.
When troops march out, they must capture,
and hold what they capture;
if they halt troops and do not attack,
they will surely be rich.
Among court officials,
the minor are not slandered,
the major are not demoted.
Prove merit to gain office and rank,
even with eloquent speech,
one cannot interfere with this,
this is called governing by rules.
Those who attack with force,
give one and take ten,
those who attack with words,
give ten and lose a hundred.
If the state values force,
this is called "attacking with difficulty";
if the state values words,
this is called "attacking with ease".
Heavy punishments and few rewards,
show the ruler loves the people,
and people die for the ruler;
heavy rewards and light punishments,
show the ruler does not love the people,
and people will not die for the ruler.
If benefits come from one source,
the state is invincible;
if from two sources,
the state gains half the benefits;
if from ten sources,
the state cannot be defended.
Heavy punishments clarify great systems,
what is not clarified,
are the six parasites.
If the six parasites form groups,
the people become useless.
Thus, in a rising state, punishments enforced make people obedient,
rewards enforced make people benefit.
Enforcing punishments,
heavily penalize minor offenses,
so minor ones do not occur,
and major ones do not come,
this is called using punishment to eliminate punishment,
punishment eliminated, tasks accomplished.
If crimes are heavy but punishments light,
punishments lead to more troubles,
this is called using punishment to invite punishment,
the state will surely decline.
The sage ruler knows the essence of things,
so his governance of people has the utmost essence.
Thus, wielding rewards and punishments to uniformly assist benevolence,
is the continuation of the heart.
The sage ruler in governing people,
must win their hearts,
thus he can use their strength.
Strength produces power,
power produces authority,
authority produces virtue,
virtue arises from strength.
The sage ruler alone possesses this,
thus he can propagate benevolence and righteousness throughout the world.
There are three factors that bring order to a state:
first, laws;
second, credibility;
third, authority.
Laws are something that both the ruler and ministers jointly uphold;
credibility is something that both the ruler and ministers jointly establish;
authority is something that the ruler alone controls.
If the ruler loses control,
there is danger;
if the ruler and ministers abandon the laws and follow personal whims,
chaos is certain.
Therefore, establishing laws and clarifying distinctions,
and not allowing personal interests to harm the laws,
leads to order;
authority and control being decided solely by the ruler
brings awe;
if the people trust in rewards, then tasks are accomplished;
if they trust in punishments, then wrongdoing has no beginning.
Only an enlightened ruler values authority and emphasizes credibility,
and does not allow personal interests to harm the laws.
Thus, if the ruler makes many generous promises but withholds rewards,
the subordinates will not be motivated;
if strict orders are repeatedly issued but punishments are not enforced,
the people will disdain crimes.
Rewards are the civil aspect;
benefits are the martial aspect.
The civil and martial aspects
are the essence of law.
Therefore, an enlightened ruler is cautious about the laws.
An enlightened ruler is called enlightened because he is not deceived;
he is called perceptive because he is not cheated.
Hence, rewards should be generous and beneficial,
punishments severe and certain,
not neglecting the distant,
nor favoring the close.
Thus, ministers do not deceive the ruler,
and subordinates do not cheat their superiors.
Those who govern in the world
often abandon the laws and rely on private opinions,
which is why states fall into chaos.
The ancient kings hung the balance and scales,
established the inch and foot,
and they are still followed today,
because their distinctions are clear.
To discard the balance and scales and judge weight,
or abolish the inch and foot and guess length,
even if perceptive,
merchants will not use them,
because they are unreliable.
Therefore, the law
is the balance and scales of the state.
Those who turn their backs on the laws and rely on private opinions
are all people who do not understand categories.
To judge wisdom, ability, worthiness, and unworthiness without using the law,
only Yáo could do it,
but the world is not all Yáo.
Thus, the ancient kings knew that self-praise and private recommendations could not be relied upon,
so they established laws and clarified distinctions,
rewarding those who met the standards,
and punishing those who undermined the public good.
The methods of reward and punishment,
if they do not lose their righteousness,
then the people do not contend.
If offices and ranks are granted
not according to one's labor,
then loyal ministers will not advance.
If rewards and salaries are distributed
not in accordance with one's achievements,
then warriors will not be used.
Generally, when ministers serve their ruler,
they often do so according to what the ruler favors.
If the ruler favors the law,
then ministers serve him with the law;
if the ruler favors rhetoric,
then ministers serve him with rhetoric.
If the ruler favors the law,
then upright scholars will be before him;
if the ruler favors rhetoric,
then slanderous and flattering ministers will be at his side.
When public and private are clearly distinguished,
then petty men do not resent the worthy,
and the unworthy do not envy achievement.
Thus, when Yáo and Shùn ruled the world,
it was not for personal gain under heaven,
but to rule the world for the world's sake.
They selected the worthy and promoted the able to pass it on,
not because they distanced themselves from their own sons,
or favored strangers,
but because they understood the way of order and chaos.
Thus, the Three Kings bonded through righteousness,
the Five Hegemons rectified the feudal lords through laws,
none seeking personal gain under heaven,
but governing the world for the world's sake.
Therefore, they held the reputation,
and achieved the merits,
the world enjoyed their governance,
and none could harm them.
Now, the rulers and ministers of this chaotic age
all presumptuously seize the benefits of the state,
and control the importance of office,
to facilitate their private interests,
which is why the state is in danger.
Thus, the boundary between public and private
is the root of survival or demise.
To abandon the laws and favor private opinions
allows treacherous ministers to sell authority for stipends,
and officials to conceal matters from below and prey on the people.
As the proverb says:
"When worms are numerous, the wood breaks;
when cracks are large, the wall collapses."
Thus, if high officials contend for private gain without regard for the people,
then the subordinates become alienated from the superiors;
such alienation
is the crack in the state.
If officials conceal matters from below to prey on the people,
this is the worm of the people.
Therefore, for a state with cracks and worms not to perish
is rare in the world.
Hence, an enlightened ruler upholds the law and rejects private interests,
and the state has no cracks or worms.
Land,
a hundred lǐ square:
mountains and hills occupy one-tenth,
marshes and lakes one-tenth,
streams, valleys, and flowing water one-tenth,
cities, towns, and paths one-tenth,
poor fields two-tenths,
good fields four-tenths,
and with this, it can support fifty thousand working men.
Its mountains, hills, marshes, lakes, streams, and valleys can supply their resources,
the cities, towns, and paths are sufficient to settle the people—
this was the rule of the ancient kings for regulating land and dividing the people.
Now the land of Qín
is five thousand lǐ square,
yet grain-producing land does not make up two-tenths,
the number of fields does not reach a million,
and the resources, goods, and treasures from its marshes, lakes, streams, valleys, famous mountains, and great rivers
are not fully utilized—
this shows that the people do not match the land.
What I mean by military forces
is not to mobilize everyone entirely;
rather, consider what within the borders can supply soldiers, chariots, and cavalry,
order the original Qín troops,
and have the new people provide fodder and food.
If there are states in the world that do not submit,
then the king can use this to disrupt their farming in spring,
consume their food in summer,
take their harvest in autumn,
and freeze their stores in winter.
Those neighboring Qín
are the Three Jìn;
the ones against whom we wish to use military force
are Hán and Wèi.
Their land is narrow and their people numerous,
their dwellings crowded together and overlapping,
and their guest settlers engage in trade and interest.
The people have no registered names above,
and no fields or dwellings below,
relying on deceitful work and secondary occupations to survive.
More than half of the people live in the shade of hills or near marshes and waters.
Use great force to shake their foundations,
and broad civil measures to pacify their successors.
If the king implements this within ten years,
the feudal lords will have no different people,
so why should the king begrudge ranks and value exemptions?
The victory of the Zhōu army,
the victory of the Huá army,
Qín cut off heads and advanced eastward.
Advancing eastward,
its lack of benefit is also clear;
yet officials still consider it a great achievement,
because it weakened the enemy.
This shows that their land is insufficient to support their people,
seemingly more so than the Qín people being insufficient to fill its land.
Considering the sentiments of the people,
what they desire
is fields and dwellings;
and it is true that Jìn has none,
while Qín has a surplus for sure.
Yet if the people do not move west under these circumstances,
it is because Qín's land is sorrowful and the people suffer.
I privately believe that the insight of Your Majesty's officials is mistaken,
which is the cause of weakness.
Not seizing the people of the Three Jìn
is due to begrudging ranks and valuing exemptions.
Their argument says:
"The reason the Three Jìn are weak
is that their people pursue pleasure and exemptions from service are lightly granted.
The reason Qín is strong
is that its people endure hardship and exemptions from service are heavily valued."
Now if ranks are granted liberally and exemptions are prolonged,
this would abandon the means by which Qín became strong,
and adopt the ways by which the Three Jìn states became weak."
Such is the argument of Your Majesty's officials who value rank and cherish exemptions,
but I humbly believe this is incorrect.
The reason for imposing hardships on the people and strengthening the military
is to attack enemies and achieve our desires.
The Art of War states:
"When the enemy is weak, our military becomes strong."
This means we do not lose our means of attack,
while the enemy loses their means of defense.
Now the Three Jìn states have not defeated Qín for four generations,
since the time of King Xiāng of Wèi,
they have never won in open battles,
their defended cities have always been captured,
in conflicts great and small,
what the Three Jìn have lost to Qín
is beyond counting.
Yet despite this they remain unsubdued,
for while Qín can seize their territory,
it cannot win over their people.
Now if Your Majesty displays enlightened benevolence,
offering that any man of the feudal states who comes to submit
shall receive three generations of exemption,
free from military service,
and that within Qín's four borders,
hills, slopes, mounds and marshes shall be exempt from taxes for ten years
as recorded in the laws,
this would suffice to feed a million farmers.
Previously I stated:
"Considering the people's sentiments,
what they truly desire
is farmland and housing;
it's certain Jìn has none available,
while Qín has plenty to spare,
yet if under these circumstances people don't move west,
it's because Qín's officers are anxious and the people suffer."
Now with the benefit of farmland and housing,
plus three generations' exemption,
this surely gives them what they want,
while sparing them what they detest.
Then surely all the people east of the mountains will move west.
Moreover, to speak plainly;
if not,
then cultivating wastelands,
producing nature's treasures,
and employing millions in fundamental occupations
would bring numerous benefits—
how could this merely preserve our offensive capacity?
What Qín worries about is that
raising troops for campaigns
impoverishes the state,
while settling peacefully for farming
allows the enemy to recuperate—
this is the dilemma Your Majesty cannot resolve.
Thus though victorious for four generations,
the world remains unsubmitted.
Now if we employ original Qín subjects against the enemy,
while putting new immigrants to fundamental work,
even if troops remain abroad for hundreds of nights,
not a moment would be lost in production at home—
this achieves both wealth and power.
Using our wild grasslands
to attract people from Three Jìn
and set them to fundamental work—
this weakens the enemy
just as victory in war does,
while Qín gains their grain production,
this is the strategy of achieving dual gains.
Consider the victories at Zhōu army,
Huá army,
and Chángpíng—
how many subjects did Qín lose?
How many soldiers and mercenaries were kept from fundamental work?
I dare say they were innumerable.
If among Your Majesty's ministers
there were one who could accomplish
with half these costs
the weakening of Jìn and strengthening of Qín
equivalent to three victories,
Your Majesty would surely reward him greatly.
Yet what I propose
requires not a day of corvée from the people,
nor countless coins from the treasury,
while weakening Jìn and strengthening Qín more than three victories would;
if Your Majesty still considers this unfeasible,
then my foolishness cannot comprehend it.
There was a man from Qí named Dōngguō Chǎng
who was full of desires,
wishing to possess ten thousand gold.
When his followers requested support,
he refused,
saying:
"I need it to buy a title."
His followers angrily left for Sòng,
saying:
"This shows no care for us,
so we're better off going where there's benefit."
Now Jìn has people,
yet Qín begrudges them exemptions—
this is loving what one doesn't have and losing what one could have,
no different from Dōngguō Chǎng's loving nonexistent wealth and losing his followers!
Moreover, antiquity had Yáo and Shùn,
praised in their time;
middle ages had Tāng and Wǔ,
reigning with popular submission.
These four kings
are hailed as sage kings through all ages,
yet their ways cannot be directly applied now.
Now with three-generation exemptions,
we can win over all people of Three Jìn—
is this not Your Majesty demonstrating worth in the present
to make later generations serve your successors?
Thus unless one is a sage, advice is rejected,
making it hard to follow sages.
Sages governing a state
unify rewards,
unify punishments,
unify education.
Unified rewards make the military invincible,
unified punishments ensure order enforcement,
unified education makes inferiors obey superiors.
Enlightened rewards are not wasteful,
enlightened punishments require no execution,
enlightened education needs no reform,
yet people understand their duties,
and the state knows no aberrant customs.
The ultimate enlightened reward
leads to no reward being needed;
the ultimate enlightened punishment
leads to no punishment being needed;
the ultimate enlightened education
leads to no education being needed.
Unified rewards mean
benefits, emoluments, offices, and ranks
come solely through military service,
with no other bestowals.
Then whether wise or foolish,
noble or base,
brave or timid,
worthy or unworthy,
all exhaust their mental knowledge,
strain their physical strength,
and would die for their ruler.
Outstanding talents follow like flowing water.
Thus the military becomes invincible
and orders prevail worldwide.
A state of ten thousand chariots
would not dare mobilize troops on the central plains;
a state of thousand chariots
would not dare defend its walls.
If a state of ten thousand chariots
dares mobilize on the central plains,
battle will destroy its army;
if a state of thousand chariots
dares defend its walls,
assault will overwhelm its city.
In battle, always destroy enemy armies;
in assault, always overwhelm enemy cities;
then all cities will be yours,
all subjects will come to you—
even with generous rewards,
what treasury exhaustion could there be?
When Tāng was enfeffed at Zànmáo,
and King Wén at Qízhōu,
their domains were merely hundred li square.
When Tāng fought Jié in the fields of Míngtiáo,
and King Wǔ fought Zhòu in the wilderness of Mùyě,
they crushed nine armies
and eventually apportioned lands to feudal lords,
with soldiers who sat in formation gaining village communities,
chariots resting unused,
horses released at Huà Mountain's south slope,
oxen freed in agricultural marshes,
left to age uncollected—
such were the rewards of Tāng and Wǔ.
Thus it is said:
Had the grain of Zànmáo and Qízhōu
been used to reward all people under heaven,
none would get even a liter;
had their money been so used,
none would get even a coin.
Therefore it is said:
Rulers of hundred-li domains
who enfeoff their ministers as marquises
greatly expand their original holdings.
Soldiers who sat in formation
gained village communities.
Why were rewards extended
even to oxen and horses?
Because
they skillfully used the wealth of all under heaven
to reward all people under heaven.
Thus it is said:
"Enlightened rewards incur no expense."
After Tāng and Wǔ had defeated Jié and Zhòu,
the land was free from harm,
and the realm was greatly stabilized.
They built the five storehouses,
stored away the five weapons,
ceased military affairs,
practiced cultural education,
set aside shields and spears,
and inserted court tablets to make music to express their virtue.
At this time,
though rewards and emoluments were not distributed,
the people remained orderly.
Thus it is said:
"The perfection of enlightened rewards
leads to the absence of rewards."
What is called uniform punishment means
there are no social ranks in punishment.
From ministers and generals down to officials and commoners,
whoever disobeys the king's commands,
violates the state's prohibitions,
or disrupts the sovereign's regulations,
shall be guilty of a capital crime without pardon.
Even if one had merit before,
but fails later,
it does not reduce the punishment.
Even if one was virtuous before,
but commits errors later,
it does not mitigate the law.
If loyal ministers or filial sons commit offenses,
they must be judged according to the measure of their crimes.
Officials who uphold the law and perform their duties,
if any fail to enforce the king's laws,
shall be guilty of a capital crime without pardon,
with punishment extending to three clans.
Colleagues in the same office
who report them to superiors
shall be exempt from punishment themselves.
Regardless of nobility or common status,
they shall inherit the official position, rank, lands, and emoluments of their superior.
Thus it is said:
"When heavy punishment connects crimes,
the people dare not test it."
Since the people dare not test it,
there is no punishment.
The former kings' prohibitions against assault and killing,
cutting off people's feet,
and tattooing people's faces
were not meant to harm the people,
but to prohibit wickedness and stop offenses.
Therefore, to prohibit wickedness and stop offenses,
nothing is better than heavy punishment.
When punishment is heavy and certain to be imposed,
the people dare not test it,
so the state has no punished people.
When the state has no punished people,
thus it is said:
"Enlightened punishment requires no execution."
Duke Wén of Jìn desired to clarify punishments to draw close to the hundred surnames,
so he assembled the feudal lords and officials at Shìqiāngōng.
Diān Jié arrived late,
and the duke requested his crime.
The ruler said:
"Carry out the matter,"
whereupon the officer broke Diān Jié's spine as an example.
The officers of Jìn,
bowing in fear, all trembled,
saying:
"Diān Jié, who was favored,
was broken as an example,
how much more so for us?"
They raised troops to attack Cáo and Wǔlù,
reversed Zhèng's breastworks,
aligned Wèi's field ridges eastward,
and defeated the Jīng people at Chéngpú.
The soldiers of the three armies,
when ordered to halt, stood as if their feet were cut off,
and when ordered to advance, moved like flowing water.
The soldiers of the three armies,
dared not violate prohibitions.
Thus, by once borrowing the way of heavy punishment through Diān Jié's spine,
Jìn was well-governed.
Formerly, Zhōu Gōng Dàn killed Guǎn Shū
and exiled Huò Shū,
saying:
"They violated prohibitions."
The multitude under heaven all said:
"Even his own brothers who erred were not spared,
how much more those distant?"
Thus all under heaven knew that knife and saw were used in Zhōu's court,
and the land was well-governed.
Thus it is said:
"The perfection of enlightened punishment
leads to the absence of punishment."
What is called uniform education means
that broad knowledge, clever debate,
trustworthiness, integrity, ritual, and music,
cultivated conduct, and forming cliques,
reputation for capability and purity,
cannot lead to wealth and honor,
cannot be used to criticize punishments,
nor can one independently present private opinions to the ruler.
The stubborn are broken,
the sharp are blunted.
Even those called sage, wise, cunning, or simple
cannot gain profit from the ruler without merit.
However, the gate to wealth and honor
lies solely in warfare.
Those who can fight
tread through the gate of wealth and honor;
the stubborn and obstructive
face constant punishment without pardon.
Therefore, fathers, brothers, acquaintances, marriage connections, and associates
all say:
"What we must devote ourselves to
is solely warfare."
Hence, the strong and adult devote themselves to battle,
the old and weak devote themselves to defense;
the dying do not regret,
the living strive to encourage.
This is what I call uniform education.
The people's desire for wealth and honor
only ceases when the coffin lid is closed.
And the gate to wealth and honor
must come from military service.
Therefore, when the people hear of war, they congratulate each other;
in their daily activities, eating and drinking, what they sing about
is war.
This is what I call
"the perfection of enlightened education,
leading to the absence of education."
This is what I call the threefold education.
The sage alone can know the essence of all things,
thus in governing the state,
he grasps the essence to reach all things.
Hence, with little education, there is much achievement.
When a sage governs a state,
it is easy to understand but difficult to practice.
Therefore, the sage need not add anything,
nor must the ordinary ruler be abolished.
Killing people is not considered brutality,
rewarding people is not considered benevolence,
because the state's laws are clear.
The sage appoints officials and confers ranks according to merit,
so the worthy do not worry.
The sage does not forgive faults,
does not pardon punishments,
so wickedness does not arise.
When a sage governs a state,
he examines only uniformity.
In the age of Kùyíng in ancient times,
they cut trees and killed beasts,
the people were few, but trees and beasts were abundant.
In the age of Huángdì,
they did not kill fawns nor take eggs,
officials had no servants for supply,
and the dead could not use outer coffins.
Affairs differed,
yet both were kings,
because the times were different.
In the age of Shénnóng,
men plowed for food,
women wove for clothing,
punishments and government were unused, yet there was order,
armor and weapons were not raised, yet he was king.
After Shénnóng passed away,
the strong overcame the weak,
the many oppressed the few.
Therefore, Huángdì established the principles of ruler and minister, high and low,
the rituals of father and son, elder and younger brother,
the union of husband and wife, consort and partner;
internally using knife and saw,
externally using armor and weapons,
because the times had changed.
From this perspective,
Shénnóng was not superior to Huángdì,
yet his name is revered
because he suited his time.
Therefore, using war to eliminate war,
even war is acceptable;
using killing to eliminate killing,
even killing is acceptable;
using punishment to eliminate punishment,
even heavy punishment is acceptable.
Those who could control the world in the past
necessarily first controlled their people;
those who could defeat strong enemies
necessarily first overcame their people.
Therefore, the foundation of controlling the people lies in governing them,
just as metal is forged,
or clay is molded.
If the foundation is not solid,
the people will be like flying birds and running beasts—
who then can control them?
The foundation of the people
is law.
Thus, those skilled in governance
restrain the people with law,
and reputation and territory are established.
Those who achieve a revered name and vast lands to become kings—
for what reason?
They are victorious in war.
Those who suffer a lowly name and diminished lands leading to ruin—
for what reason?
They are defeated in war.
To become king without victory,
or to perish without defeat—
from ancient times to the present,
such has never occurred.
When the people are brave,
war is won;
when the people are not brave,
war is lost.
Those who can unify the people in war
make them brave;
those who cannot unify the people in war
leave them not brave.
The sage kings saw that kingship is achieved through military might,
so they directed the entire state to prioritize it.
Enter a state,
observe its governance—
if the people are utilized, it is strong.
How can one tell the people are being utilized?
When the people see battle,
like hungry wolves seeing meat,
then they are being utilized.
Generally, war
is what the people detest;
those who can make the people delight in war
become kings.
In managing the ranks,
organize them in groups of five,
distinguish them with insignias,
bind them with orders—
so that incompetence has no place,
and negligence finds no birth.
Thus, the masses of the three armies
follow orders like flowing water,
facing death without turning back.
When a state is in chaos,
it is not that its laws are chaotic,
nor that laws are not applied.
Every state has laws,
but lacks the laws to ensure laws are enforced.
Every state has laws against treachery, evil, and theft,
but lacks the laws to ensure traitors and thieves are always caught.
Those who commit treachery or theft
face the death penalty,
yet if treachery and theft do not cease,
it is because they are not always caught.
If they are always caught,
and treachery and theft still persist,
the punishment is too light.
Light punishments
fail to eradicate crime.
Ensuring capture
means many are punished.
Thus, skilled governors
punish the wicked,
but do not reward the good,
so without punishment, the people become good.
Without punishment and the people being good—
it is due to severe penalties.
Severe penalties
make the people dare not offend,
hence no punishments are needed.
And if none dare do wrong,
the whole state becomes good.
Therefore, without rewarding goodness,
the people are good.
Rewarding goodness is unnecessary,
just as rewarding non-theft is.
Thus, skilled governors
can make even Zhí trustworthy,
let alone Bóyí?
Inept governors
make even Bóyí suspect,
let alone Zhí?
If circumstances prevent wrongdoing,
even Zhí can be trusted;
if circumstances allow wrongdoing,
even Bóyí becomes suspect.
States may be highly ordered,
or deeply chaotic.
With an enlightened ruler above,
appointments are always worthy,
so law resides in the worthy;
law residing in the worthy
means law prevails below,
and the unworthy dare not do wrong—
this is called high order.
With an unenlightened ruler above,
appointments are always unworthy;
the state lacks clear laws,
the unworthy dare to do wrong—
this is called deep chaos.
Militarily, states may be doubly strong,
or doubly weak.
If the people inherently desire to fight,
and have no choice but to fight,
this is called doubly strong.
If the people inherently do not desire to fight,
and can avoid fighting,
this is called doubly weak.
Enlightened rulers do not lavishly enrich or ennoble their ministers.
What is called wealth
is not grain, pearls, or jade;
what is called nobility
is not rank or office,
but abolishing law for private grants of wealth and nobility.
Generally, a ruler's actions are not superior to others,
his wisdom not beyond others,
his courage and strength not surpassing others.
Yet even with sagely wisdom, the people dare not plot against me;
with courage and strength, they dare not kill me;
though numerous, they dare not overcome their ruler;
even with people numbering in the millions,
heavy rewards are posted but none dare contend,
punishments are carried out but none dare complain—
it is due to law.
In a chaotic state,
the people have many private righteousnesses;
in a weak military,
the people have much private bravery,
leading to decline.
If the paths to obtaining ranks and emoluments in a state are many,
it leads to ruin.
The desires of a perishing state
devalue ranks and scorn emoluments,
eating without laboring,
gaining honor without fighting,
being respected without rank,
wealthy without emolument,
leading without office—
these are called treacherous people.
It is said a well-governed ruler has no loyal ministers,
a kind father has no filial sons.
They wish not for good words,
all are supervised by law,
corrected by commands,
unable to do wrong alone,
and none will join them in wrongdoing.
What is called wealth
is much income and little expenditure.
If clothing and food are regulated,
eating and drinking moderated,
then expenditure is little.
If women's duties are fully done inside,
men's duties fully done outside,
then income is much.
What is called enlightenment
is leaving nothing unseen,
so ministers dare not commit treachery,
the common people dare not do wrong.
Thus, the ruler sits upon a comfortable couch,
listens to the sounds of strings and pipes,
and the world is well-governed.
What is called enlightenment
compels the masses to act.
What is called strength
conquers the world;
conquering the world
thus unites forces.
So the brave and strong dare not commit violence,
the wise and sagely dare not be deceitful.
And considering the multitude across the world,
none dare not do what he favors,
and avoid what he detests.
What is called strength
compels courage and might to serve oneself.
If his will is fulfilled,
the world benefits him;
if unfulfilled,
the world pleases him.
Those who rely on the world
are abandoned by it;
those who rely on themselves
gain the world.
He who gains the world,
first gains himself;
he who can defeat a strong enemy,
first overcomes himself.
The sage knows the inevitable principles,
and the circumstances that must be acted upon;
thus he implements governance that ensures order,
leads people who are inevitably courageous in battle,
and issues commands that are inevitably obeyed.
Hence, when the army marches out, it has no rival;
when orders are issued, the world submits.
The flight of the yellow swan,
covering a thousand miles in one soar,
is due to its inherent preparedness for flight.
Qílín and Lù'ěr,
traveling a thousand miles a day,
possess the inherent momentum for running.
Tigers, leopards, bears, and brown bears,
fierce and unrivaled,
have the inevitable principle of victory.
The sage perceives the fundamental nature of governance,
knows the inevitable principles,
thus in governing the people,
he is like using height to control water,
or using dryness and dampness to control fire.
Therefore it is said:
The benevolent can practice benevolence toward others,
but cannot make others benevolent;
The righteous can love others,
but cannot make others loving.
Thus it is known that benevolence and righteousness are insufficient to govern the world.
The sage has an inherently trustworthy nature,
and also possesses laws that compel the world to trust.
What is called righteousness
is loyalty as a minister,
filial piety as a son,
propriety between young and old,
and distinction between men and women;
if it is not righteous,
one would not eat even when starving,
nor cling to life in the face of death.
This is the constant practice under law.
The sage king
does not value righteousness but values law—
laws must be clear,
commands must be enforced,
and that is all.
Within the four borders,
all men and women are registered with the state,
the living are listed,
the dead are removed.
Those with rank may request those without rank to serve as Shùzǐ,
one per rank.
When there are no corvée duties,
the Shùzǐ serve their Dàfū,
six days a month;
when there are corvée duties,
they follow and support them.
Military ranks,
from the first level down to Xiǎofū,
are called Jiàotú Cāoshì.
Civil ranks,
from the second level up to Bùgēng,
are called Zú.
In battle,
five men are organized into a squad;
if one dies,
the other four are beheaded.
If they can capture one head each,
they are reinstated.
Five squads have one Túnzhǎng,
one hundred men have one Jiàng.
In battle,
the Jiàng and Túnzhǎng must achieve decapitations;
if they obtain thirty-three heads or more,
meeting the quota,
the Jiàng and Túnzhǎng are granted one rank.
A commander of five hundred,
has fifty close guards.
Two units of five hundred,
commanded by a general,
have one hundred close guards.
A magistrate of a thousand shí,
has one hundred close guards.
A magistrate of eight hundred shí,
has eighty close guards.
A magistrate of seven hundred shí,
has seventy close guards.
A magistrate of six hundred shí,
has sixty close guards.
The Guówèi,
has a thousand close guards.
The Dàjiàng,
has four thousand close guards.
If they die in battle or duty,
their close guards are beheaded;
if they can capture one head each,
they are reinstated.
If they can besiege a city and behead over eight thousand,
they meet the quota;
in field battles, beheading two thousand,
meets the quota.
Officials from Cāoshì up to Dàjiàng,
are all rewarded among the military officers.
Thus, the rank of Gōngshì
advances to Shàngzào.
Thus, the rank of Shàngzào
advances to Zānniǎo.
Thus, the rank of Zānniǎo
advances to Bùgēng.
Thus, the rank of Bùgēng
advances to Dàfū.
An official with rank appointed as Xiànwèi,
is granted captives,
and six plus five thousand six hundred.
A Dàfū with rank appointed as Guówèi,
advances to Guāndàfū.
Thus, the rank of Guāndàfū
advances to Gōngdàfū.
Thus, the rank of Gōngdàfū
advances to Gōngchéng.
Thus, the rank of Gōngchéng
advances to Wǔdàfū,
then granted a tax domain of three hundred households.
Thus, the rank of Wǔdàfū
advances to Shùzhǎng;
thus, the rank of Shùzhǎng
advances to Zuǒgēng;
thus, the rank of Sāngēng
advances to Dàliángzào
—all are granted a fief of three hundred households,
and a tax domain of three hundred households.
A Wǔdàfū with a tax domain of six hundred households
may retain retainers.
The Dàjiàng's chariot drivers and assistants,
are all granted three ranks.
Thus, a Kèqīng who meets the quota in evaluation,
advances to Zhèngqīng.
Due to battle,
exposing heads for three days,
then reviewing for three days,
the general, without doubt, awards the Shìdàfū with merit ranks.
As for merit ranks,
if a county exceeds three days,
and fails to award the Shìdàfū with merit ranks,
it is capable.

evaluated by the Chéngwèi,
those who can obtain one armored head,
are rewarded with one rank,
one qǐng of additional land,
and nine mǔ of additional residence land.
Per rank, one Shùzǐ is exempted,
then they may enter as military officials.
As for legal procedures:
high ranks may demote lower ranks.
High ranks, if capable,
are not assigned servants of ranked persons.
Ranks from the second level and above,
if convicted of a crime, are demoted.
Ranks from the first level and below,
if convicted of a crime, are stripped.
From the death of a Xiǎofū,
up to Dàfū,
their official rank one level,
their grave trees one tree per rank.
In besieging a city,
the Guó Sīkōng evaluates the city's width and thickness;
the Guówèi allocates areas, and the Túxiào divide the cubic feet for attack,
setting a deadline:
"Those who finish first,
shall be deemed the vanguard;
those who finish last,
shall be deemed the rearguard;
if evaluated twice as such, they are dismissed."
When tunnels are through, accumulate firewood,
accumulate firewood then burn the pillars.
The assault troops,
eighteen men per front.
The assault troops know to fight fiercely,
if they behead five enemy troops,
then the assault troops,
each are granted one rank.
If they die,
one person succeeds them;
if they fail to fight to the death,
a thousand people circle to watch,
and they are tattooed and have noses cut off beneath the city wall.
The Guówèi allocates areas,
with central troops following.
The general sets up a wooden platform,
with the Guó Zhèngjiān,
and the king's Yùshǐ,
observing together from it.
Those who enter first
are recommended as the foremost;
those who enter later
are recommended as the rearmost.
When storming enemy formations,
use all those willing;
if the willing are insufficient,
then supplement them with the next in line.
When the people are weak, the state is strong;
when the people are strong, the state is weak.
Therefore, a state with the Way
focuses on weakening the people.
Simplicity leads to strength,
indulgence leads to weakness;
weakness ensures conformity,
indulgence fosters wayward ambitions;
weakness makes them useful,
wayward ambitions make them strong.
Hence it is said:
"Using strength to eliminate weakness results in weakness,
using weakness to eliminate strength results in strength."
If the people are treated kindly, they become harmonious;
if given benefits, they become useful;
being useful means they can be assigned tasks,
harmony leads to scarcity;
having tasks enriches governance.
If the ruler abandons laws
and lets the people follow their preferences,
then villainy multiplies.
When the people are poor, they strive for wealth;
when wealthy, they become indulgent;
indulgence breeds parasites.
Thus, if the people are wealthy but not utilized,
make them earn ranks with grain;
ranks must be obtained through their labor,
so farmers do not slack.
If farmers do not slack,
the six parasites cannot sprout.
Thus, the state grows rich and the people are orderly,
achieving double strength.
Military strength is easily weakened but hard to strengthen;
the people enjoy life and comfort,
making death and hardship hard to enforce;
changing this brings strength.
If affairs have shame,
villainy decreases;
if rewards are faultless,
villainy becomes doubtful.
Enemy mistakes must be exploited,
then the army gains supreme power.
If affairs lack shame,
use warfare advantageously;
long maintaining advantageous positions,
one will surely rule.
Thus, an army that does what the enemy dares not do
is strong;
undertaking what the enemy is ashamed to do
brings profit.
With laws established,
the people settle in their roles;
if the ruler adapts,
affairs achieve balance;
the state maintains stability,
the ruler wields power and profit.
Hence, the ruler values frequent changes,
the state values few changes.
If profit comes from one source,
the state has abundant goods;
from ten sources,
the state has scarce goods.
Upholding one brings order,
upholding ten brings chaos.
Order leads to strength,
chaos to weakness;
strength attracts goods,
weakness drives them away.
Thus, a state that gathers goods is strong,
one that loses them is weak.
When humiliated, the people value ranks;
when weak, they respect officials;
when poor, they prize rewards.
Governing with punishment makes them willing tools,
using rewards to fight makes them scorn death.
Hence, being prepared for war and having usable troops is called strength.
If the people have private honor,
they disdain ranks and despise officials;
if wealthy, they轻视rewards.
Governing by shaming the people,
using punishment in war ensures they fight.
If the people fear death and affairs are chaotic when fighting,
then soldiers and farmers slacken, and the state weakens.
Farmers, merchants, and officials—these three
are the state's constant offices.
Farmers open lands,
merchants bring goods,
officials govern the people.
These three offices produce six parasites:
the year,
food,
beauty,
finery,
ambitions,
and conduct.
If these six have simplicity,
the state will surely decline.
If farmers have surplus food,
they idly pass the year.
If merchants have excessive profits,
they damage utensils with beauty and finery.
If officials are appointed but unused,
ambitions and conduct become reckless.
If the six parasites become customs,
the army will surely be greatly defeated.
If laws are crooked, governance is chaotic;
appointing the virtuous leads to many words;
with complex governance, the state is chaotic;
many words weaken the military.
If laws are clear, governance is simple;
appointing the capable silences words;
simple governance brings state order;
silenced words strengthen the military.
Thus, governing a large state
requires small methods;
governing a small state
requires large methods.
If policies enforce what the people hate,
the people are weak;
if policies follow what the people enjoy,
the people are strong.
Weak people mean a strong state;
strong people mean a weak state.
Policies following what the people enjoy
make the people strong;
if the people are strong and strengthened further,
the military becomes doubly weak.
Policies enforcing what the people hate
make the people weak;
if the people are weak and weakened further,
the military becomes doubly strong.
Thus, using strength to double weakness
leads to decline;
using weakness to double strength
leads to kingship.
Using strength to attack strength
results in weakness,
with strength preserved;
using weakness to attack weakness
results in strength,
with strength removed.
If strength is preserved, decline follows;
if strength is removed, kingship follows.
Hence, using strength to attack weakness
brings decline;
using weakness to attack strength
brings kingship.
An enlightened ruler in employing ministers
ensures appointments are based on merit,
and rewards fully match their labor.
If a ruler makes his people trust him like the sun and moon,
he will be invincible.
Even if Lí Lóu could see the tip of an autumn hair,
he could not give his keen sight to others;
even if Wū Huò could lift a thousand jun,
he could not give his great strength to others;
even a sage's inherent nature
cannot be exchanged with others.
Those in power today
all wish to be supreme sages,
which means upholding the law.
Governing by背离laws
is like a heavy burden and long road without horses or oxen,
or crossing a great river without boat or oar.
Now, having numerous people and a strong army
is a great asset for an emperor.
But without clear laws to protect it,
one neighbors peril and ruin.
Thus, enlightened rulers scrutinize laws.
Within the borders, the people
have no wicked or indulgent hearts;
wandering scholars
are compelled into battle formations;
the masses toil diligently at farming—
there is a way to know this is so.
The people of the state of Chǔ,
swift and uniform,
move rapidly like a whirlwind;
their Yuán iron spears,
sharp as bee or scorpion stings;
armored in rhinoceros hide,
firm as metal or stone.
With the Jiāng and Hàn as their moats,
the Rǔ and Yǐng as their boundaries,
shielded by the Dèng Forest,
bordered by the Fāngchéng walls.
The Qín army reached Yānyǐng,
capturing it as easily as shaking dead leaves,
Táng Miè died at Chuíshā,
Zhuāng Qiāo rose up from within,
and Chǔ was divided into five parts.
Its territory was not small,
its soldiers were not few,
and its armor, weapons, and resources were not insufficient.
Yet it could not win in battle,
nor hold firm in defense.
This arose from the lack of strict laws.
Chapter 27: Governing Banditry
Among the people's external affairs,
none is harder than warfare,
so lenient laws cannot prepare them for it.
What are lenient laws?
They mean meager rewards and weak authority,
and the failure to block corrupting paths.
What are corrupting paths?
They refer to honoring the eloquent and clever,
employing itinerant officials,
and promoting literary pursuits and personal fame.
If these three are not blocked,
the people will avoid battle and affairs will fail.
Thus, with meager rewards,
those who listen see no benefit;
with weak authority,
those who violate see no harm.
So, opening corrupting paths to lure them,
and using lenient laws to make them fight,
is like setting a trap for mice with a cat as bait—
is it not almost futile?
Therefore, to make one's people fight,
one must use heavy laws,
—rewards must be plentiful,
authority must be severe;
corrupting paths must be blocked,
—the eloquent and clever
must not be honored,
itinerant officials must not be employed,
and literary pursuits and personal fame must not be promoted.
With plentiful rewards and severe authority,
the people, seeing the abundance of battle rewards, will forget death;
seeing the disgrace of not fighting, they will suffer in life.
Rewards make them forget death,
and authority makes them suffer in life,
while corrupting paths are blocked.
Facing the enemy with this,
is like shooting a drifting leaf with a hundred-dàn crossbow—
what could it not penetrate?
Among the people's internal affairs,
none is harder than farming,
so lenient governance cannot motivate them.
What is lenient governance?
It means farmers are poor and merchants rich,
so food is cheap and money valuable.
Cheap food makes farmers poor,
valuable money makes merchants rich;
if non-essential activities are not prohibited,
then skilled craftsmen profit,
and idle eaters multiply.
Thus, farmers labor most bitterly,
yet cannot match merchants and craftsmen.
If one can prevent merchants and craftsmen from proliferating,
then even wishing the state not to be wealthy
would be impossible.
Therefore, to enrich the state through farming,
food within the borders must be expensive,
taxes on non-farmers must be heavy,
and market profits must be highly taxed,
so the people cannot avoid farming.
Without farmland,
they must exchange for food;
expensive food benefits farmers,
benefiting farmers makes many pursue it.
With expensive food,
buying grain is unprofitable,
and heavy taxes are imposed,
so the people must abandon commerce and craftsmanship
and work the land.
Thus, all the people's profits lie in land benefits.
Therefore, a ruler
should direct all border profits to the military,
and all market profits to farming.
Directing all border profits to the military
brings strength;
directing all market profits to farming
brings wealth.
Thus, strong in battle
and wealthy at rest
leads to kingship.
