In ancient times, before rulers and subjects, high and low existed,
the people were chaotic and ungoverned.
Thus, the sages distinguished noble and base,
established ranks and positions,
and set up titles
to define the principles of ruler and subject, high and low.
With vast land,
numerous people,
and abundant goods,
they appointed five officials to guard them.
With numerous people, wickedness arose,
so they established laws, regulations, and standards to prohibit it.
Therefore, the principles of ruler and subject,
the divisions of the five officials,
and the prohibitions of laws and regulations
must be carefully upheld.
If one holds the ruler's position but commands are not followed,
it is perilous;
if the five officials are divided but without constant duties,
it brings chaos;
if laws are set but private favors prevail,
the people will not fear punishment.
When the ruler is revered, commands are followed;
when officials are well-ordered, duties are constant;
when laws are clear, the people fear punishment.
If laws are unclear,
and one expects the people to obey orders,
it is impossible.
If the people do not obey orders,
and one seeks the ruler's reverence,
even with the wisdom of Yáo and Shùn,
they could not govern.
An enlightened king governs the world
by following the law in governance,
and rewarding according to merit.
Whenever the people fight fiercely and do not avoid death,
it is to seek rank and emolument.
An enlightened ruler governs the state
so that soldiers with merits of beheading or capturing enemies
have ranks truly honorable
and emoluments truly sufficient.
Farmers who do not leave their fields
can support both parents
and supply military needs.
Thus, soldiers die with integrity,
and farmers do not neglect their duties.
Modern rulers are not so.
They abandon laws for cleverness,
and disregard merit for reputation.
So soldiers do not fight,
and farmers wander displaced.
I hear that the way to guide the people
lies in what the ruler prioritizes.
Thus, the people can be made to farm and fight,
or to be itinerant officials,
or to pursue learning.
It depends on what the ruler grants—
if the ruler grants based on merit,
the people will fight;
if the ruler grants based on poetry and books,
the people will pursue learning.
The people's pursuit of profit
is like water flowing downward,
choosing no direction.
Whatever the people can do to gain profit,
the ruler grants it.
Those who glare, clench wrists, and speak of bravery gain it,
those who dress elegantly and debate gain it,
those who spend long years accumulating service in private circles gain it.
Honoring these three types,
who gain without merit,
the people abandon farming and fighting for them,
some seeking through debate,
some requesting through flattery,
some contending through bravery.
Thus, farmers and fighters dwindle daily,
while idle eaters multiply,
leading to state chaos and territory loss,
military weakness and ruler humiliation.
This happens because
they abandon laws and regulations for reputation.
Therefore, an enlightened ruler carefully upholds laws and regulations.
Words not conforming to law
are not heeded;
actions not conforming to law
are not honored;
affairs not conforming to law
are not undertaken.
Words conforming to law
are heeded;
actions conforming to law
are honored;
affairs conforming to law
are undertaken.
Thus, the state is well-governed and territory expands,
the military is strong and the ruler revered.
This is the pinnacle of governance,
which rulers must not fail to examine.
The means by which a ruler enforces prohibitions and commands
are rewards and punishments.
Rewards follow merit,
punishments follow crimes;
therefore, in assessing merit and investigating crimes,
one cannot but be meticulous.
To reward the noble and punish the lowly
without the ruler necessarily understanding the method
is the same as having no method at all.
All who understand the Way
rely on strategic advantage and method.
Thus, the former kings did not rely on their strength,
but on their strategic advantage;
they did not rely on trust,
but on method.
Consider tumbleweed,
which travels a thousand li when met with a whirlwind,
by riding the momentum of the wind.
Those who sound the depths know the abyss is a thousand fathoms deep,
by the method of suspending a rope.
Therefore, those who rely on strategic advantage
will reach their goal no matter how distant;
those who adhere to method
will obtain it no matter how deep.
In the dark of night,
even the great mountains and hills,
Lí Lóu could not see;
but in the clear dawn with the sun rising,
he could distinguish birds flying above
and inspect the finest autumn down below.
Thus, the ability of the eyes to see
relies on the advantage of sunlight.
When strategic advantage is maximized,
one needs no additional officials to achieve purity,
and by applying method, affairs are handled appropriately.
Now, relying on numerous officials and clerks,
with deputies and supervisors established,
the purpose of setting up deputies and supervisors
is to prevent people from pursuing profit;
but if deputies and supervisors also seek profit,
then how can they restrain each other?
Therefore, governing by relying on deputies and supervisors
is a governance that barely survives.
Those who understand method do otherwise:
they differentiate strategic advantages,
making the path difficult.
Hence it is said:
"When the situation makes concealment difficult,
even Zhí would not commit wrongdoing."
Thus, the former kings valued strategic advantage.
Some say:
"If the ruler holds emptiness and follows behind to respond,
then things will correspond and be verified,
and verification will expose villainy."
Your servant disagrees.
When officials make decisions autocratically a thousand li away,
with annual reports finalized in the twelfth month,
and affairs are accounted for yearly,
while the ruler listens to them all at once,
if doubts arise,
they cannot be concealed,
yet the personnel are insufficient.
When things are present,
the eyes cannot help but see them;
when words are close,
the ears cannot help but hear them.
Thus, when things are present, they are discerned;
when words arrive, they are discussed.
Therefore, in a well-governed state's system,
the people cannot evade crime,
just as the eyes cannot hide what they see from the mind.
Now, disordered states are not so;
they rely on numerous officials and clerks.
Though officials are many,
their affairs and interests are identical.
When affairs and interests are identical,
mutual supervision is impossible.
Moreover, differing benefits and separate harms
are what the former kings used for security.
Thus, in the highest order of governance,
even husband and wife or friends cannot cover up each other's faults or conceal wrongs,
without harming their closeness,
and the people cannot hide for one another.
The ruler and his officials
share tasks but have conflicting interests.
Consider the horse keeper and the trainer:
they cannot supervise each other,
because their tasks are shared and interests aligned.
If horses could speak,
then the keeper and trainer could not escape exposure of their faults,
due to differing interests.
When interests align and faults are shared,
a father cannot inquire of his son,
nor a ruler of his minister.
Official to official,
interests align and faults are shared.
Those who share tasks but have conflicting interests
are what the former kings used as a foundation.
When the people deceive the ruler,
without harm from concealment,
the worthy cannot add to it,
nor the unworthy diminish it.
Thus, discarding worthies and wisdom
is the method of governance.
Every age tends to govern using what actually causes disorder.
So, minor governance leads to minor disorder,
major governance to major disorder.
If rulers cannot govern their people generationally,
there has never been a state free from disorder.
What does it mean to govern using what causes disorder?
Promoting the worthy and capable
is how the age seeks order;
yet it is why order turns to disorder.
Those deemed worthy by the age
are called upright in speech;
but the reason for their upright speech
is factionalism.
Hearing their words,
one thinks them capable;
asking their faction,
one agrees.
Thus, they are honored
without waiting for achievements;
punished,
without waiting for crimes.
This situation
precisely enables corrupt officials to have the means to accomplish their villainy and risks,
and petty men to have the means to exercise their cunning schemes.
Initially lending officials and people the root of cunning schemes,
yet seeking honest ends from them—
even Yǔ could not command a group of ten men this way,
how can an ordinary ruler control the people of a state?
Those who form factions with others
do not need me to accomplish their affairs.
When the ruler promotes one and the people,
the people turn their backs on the ruler's position and lean toward private connections.
If the people turn from the ruler to private ties,
then the ruler is weakened and the ministers strengthened.
If the ruler does not discern this,
he will either be invaded by feudal lords
or overthrown by the common people.
The trend of rhetoric and persuasion
is studied by both foolish and wise alike.
If scholars learn from rhetoricians,
then the people abandon practical affairs and recite empty words.
When the people abandon practical matters for empty talk,
strength diminishes and criticism multiplies.
If the ruler does not discern this,
in war, he will surely lose his generals;
in defense, he will sell out his cities.
Therefore, if enlightened rulers and loyal ministers arise in this age
and can lead their state,
they must not forget the law for a moment.
Defeat and overcome cliques and appointments,
eliminate and reduce empty talk,
and govern by relying on the law.
Make it so that officials have no means to uphold anything without the law,
then even the clever cannot commit villainy;
make it so that the people have no way to utilize their abilities except in war,
then even the risky cannot scheme.
Governing each other by law,
promoting each other by method,
praise cannot benefit one another,
slander cannot harm one another.
When the people see that mutual praise brings no benefit,
they will oversee and report evils;
seeing that slander causes no harm,
they become accustomed to mutual dislike without mutual injury.
Those who love others do not flatter,
those who hate others do not harm;
each acts with correctness—
this is the pinnacle of governance.
Therefore, your servant says:
"When the law is employed, the state is well-governed."
A state of a thousand chariots that can defend itself
preserves its existence;
a state of ten thousand chariots that can wage war
maintains its integrity;
even with a tyrant like Jié as ruler,
he would not utter half a word of submission to his enemy.
If unable to fight externally
or defend internally,
even with Yáo as ruler,
he could not avoid submitting to a state deemed inferior.
From this perspective,
what makes a state weighty,
and a ruler respected,
is power.
In these two aspects,
power is fundamental.
Yet rulers of the age cannot focus on developing power;
why is that?
Because they make farming the bitterest toil for the people,
and warfare the most perilous.
There are two things:
a filial son finds it difficult to serve his parents,
and a loyal minister finds it difficult to serve his ruler.
Now, if one wishes to drive the masses
to do what even filial sons and loyal ministers find difficult,
I believe it cannot be done without coercing them with punishments
and driving them with rewards.
Yet nowadays, those who govern according to common practice
all abandon laws and regulations and rely on cleverness and wisdom,
neglecting military achievements and promoting benevolence and righteousness,
so the people do not devote themselves to farming and warfare.
If the people do not direct their efforts to agriculture,
then food will be scarce internally;
if they do not commit their loyalty to warfare,
then the military will be weak externally.
Internally, food is scarce;
externally, the military is weak.
Even with a territory of ten thousand li
and a million armored soldiers,
it is as if standing alone on a plain.
Moreover, the former kings could make their people tread on sharp blades
and face arrows and stones.
Their people desired to do so
not because they enjoyed learning it,
but to avoid harm.
Therefore, I teach that those who seek profit
can only obtain it through farming;
those who wish to avoid harm
can only escape it through warfare.
Within the borders, all the people
must first engage in farming and warfare to attain what they desire.
Thus, with little land, grain is abundant;
with few people, the military is strong.
If these two can be implemented within the state,
then the way of hegemony is complete.
The duke asked Gōngsūn Yāng:
"If laws and decrees are established according to the times,
and the next morning you wish to make all officials and people in the world
clearly understand and apply them uniformly without partiality,
how can this be done?"
Gōngsūn Yāng replied:
Appoint officials and clerks for the laws and decrees who are sufficiently straightforward to understand the meaning of the laws,
and those who are deemed upright for the world
shall be reported to the Son of Heaven;
the Son of Heaven names them,
then those in charge of the laws and decrees for the people
all descend to receive orders and are dispatched to offices.
Each person in charge of the laws and decrees for the people
who dares to forget the names specified by the laws they oversee,
shall be punished
according to the forgotten law or decree.
If an official in charge of laws and decrees is transferred or dies,
immediately have a student read the meaning of the laws and decrees,
set a standard procedure,
and make them understand the meaning within a few days;
if they fail to meet the standard,
establish a law to punish them.
Anyone who dares to alter a law or decree,
changing even one character or more,
shall be punished with death without pardon.
When any official or people ask the official in charge about the meaning of a law or decree,
they must clearly inform them according to the law they intended to ask about.
Prepare a tally of one chi six cun in length,
inscribed with the year, month, day, time, and the name of the law inquired about,
to inform the officials and people.
If the official in charge of laws and decrees
does not inform the officials and people of the meaning of the law they asked about,
they shall be punished
with the penalty of the law the officials and people inquired about.
Then give the left tally to the officials or people who asked about the law,
while the official in charge of laws and decrees
carefully stores the right tally in a wooden box,
keeps it in a room,
and seals it with the long seal of the laws and decrees.
If later there is a death,
proceed according to the tally document.
All laws and decrees shall have duplicates:
one duplicate in the Son of Heaven's palace,
establish a prohibited room for the laws and decrees,
with locks as restrictions and sealed,
storing the laws and decrees inside;
another duplicate in the prohibited room,
sealed with a prohibition seal.
Anyone who dares to break the seal of the prohibited room,
or enters the prohibited room to view the restricted laws and decrees,
or alters even one character of the restrictions,
shall be punished with death without pardon.
Once a year, receive the laws and decrees according to the prohibitions.
The Son of Heaven appoints three legal judges;
one judge in the palace,
one judge and clerk in the censorate,
one judge in the chancellor's office,
and each feudal lord, commandery, and county shall have one judge and clerk appointed,
all comparable to the Qin judges.
Once the commanderies, counties, and feudal lords receive the laws from the prohibited room,
they also study their meanings.
Officials and people who wish to know the laws and decrees
all ask the judges,
so all officials and people in the world
know the laws.
Officials clearly know that the people understand the laws and decrees,
so they dare not treat the people unlawfully,
and the people dare not break the law to confront the judges.
If an official treats people without following the law,
the people ask the judge,
and the judge informs them of the legal penalty,
then the people formally notify the official with the judge's words.
Officials know this,
so they dare not treat the people unlawfully,
and the people dare not break the law.
Thus,
all officials and people in the world,
even if virtuous, eloquent, and wise,
dare not utter a word to distort the law;
even with a thousand pieces of gold,
they cannot use a single zhu.
Therefore, the knowledgeable, virtuous, and capable all act with goodness,
all striving to govern themselves and uphold public duty,
and the people, even if ignorant, are easy to govern.
This all arises from laws that are clear, easy to understand, and must be enforced.
Laws and decrees
are the life of the people,
the foundation of governance,
and the means to protect the people.
To govern without laws and decrees
is like wanting to avoid hunger by abandoning food,
wanting to avoid cold by discarding clothing,
or wanting to go east by heading west—
it is clearly unachievable.
One rabbit runs,
a hundred people chase it,
not for the rabbit itself.
Yet sellers fill the market,
and thieves dare not take,
because ownership is already determined.
Thus, when ownership is undetermined,
even Yáo, Shùn, Yǔ, and Tāng would all chase like [horses];
when ownership is determined,
even greedy thieves do not take.
Now, if laws and decrees are unclear,
and their definitions unsettled,
people in the world can debate them,
with opinions varying and uncertain.
The ruler makes laws above,
while the people debate below,
leading to unstable laws and decrees,
with inferiors acting as superiors.
This is what is called undefined ownership.
When ownership is undefined,
even Yáo and Shùn would bend and act treacherously,
let alone ordinary people?
This causes great rise of treachery and evil,
the ruler loses authority and power,
leading to the path of national ruin and destruction of the altars of land and grain.
Now, when ancient sages wrote books
and passed them to later generations,
they must be taught by masters,
then one knows the so-called names;
without learning from masters,
and people interpreting them with their own minds,
they may die without knowing the names and meanings.
Therefore, sages must appoint officials for laws and decrees,
appoint clerks,
to be teachers for the world,
in order to define ownership.
When ownership is defined,
then the great are faithful and sincere,
the people are honest and diligent,
and each governs themselves.
Thus, with ownership defined,
it is the way of orderly governance;
with ownership undefined,
it is the way of chaos.
So, orderly governance cannot be disrupted,
and chaos cannot be governed.
Trying to govern chaos only increases disorder,
while governing order leads to stability.
Thus, sage kings govern order, not chaos.
Subtle and intentional words
are difficult even for the wisest.
Without the straightedge of laws and decrees, yet achieving perfect correctness
is one in ten thousand.
Therefore, sages govern the world for the ten thousand.
So, only the wise can understand afterward,
but this cannot be made law,
for not all people are knowledgeable;
only the virtuous can understand afterward,
but this cannot be made law,
for not all people are virtuous.
Thus, when sages create laws,
they must make them clear and easy to understand,
so that names are correct, and both foolish and wise can comprehend them.
Appoint legal judges,
set up officials in charge of laws as teachers for the world,
to prevent the myriad people from falling into danger and peril.
Thus, when a sage establishes order in the world without having to execute anyone,
it is not that punishments or killings are not applied,
but because the laws and decrees are clear and easily understood.
He appoints legal officials as teachers to guide the people,
ensuring that all know what to avoid and what to embrace.
They avoid misfortune and pursue blessings, thereby governing themselves.
Hence, an enlightened ruler builds upon this self-governance to achieve ultimate order,
and so the world attains great harmony.
